refuted.name: Audit for the fp16 loss-scale overflow that permanently poisons Muon/NorMuon momentum
refuted.realistic_gain: Zero. Both named failure modes are structurally impossible in this trainer, and the third premise (that it would be silent) is false here. Three greps of runs/ultra/metrics.jsonl confirm the run is clean in about two minutes. The one residual item, reordering the Newton-Schulz normalization into fp32, is a strict precision improvement worth well under 0.1% of loss and should ride along at the next unavoidable restart, not justify one.
refuted.reasoning:
The DeepSpeed bug is real but it is a DeepSpeed ZeRO architecture bug, not a Muon bug. Issue #8432 places muon_update inside get_flat_partition, called from independent_gradient_partition_epilogue, which is the gradient-reduction epilogue and runs BEFORE the fp16 engine's overflow check. That fusion is what lets a poisoned momentum survive. MaxGPT-Ultra does not use DeepSpeed.

Fix 1 (momentum updated before the skip decision) does not apply. train/trainer.py:train_step uses torch.amp.GradScaler: scaler.unscale_(optimizer), then clip_grad_norm_, then scaler.step(optimizer). train/muon.py's Muon is a plain torch.optim.Optimizer and does not set _step_supports_amp_scaling, so GradScaler takes the gated path. In torch 2.7's torch/amp/grad_scaler.py, _maybe_opt_step is: "retval = None; if not sum(v.item() for v in optimizer_state['found_inf_per_device'].values()): retval = optimizer.step(*args, **kwargs); return retval". On an overflow step, Muon.step() is never entered at all, so buf.mul_().add_(g), st["row_v"] and the AdamW moments are all untouched. Nothing can be folded in. (The codebase also uses heavy-ball buf.mul_(mom).add_(g), not DeepSpeed's momentum.lerp_(grad, 1-beta), and never writes momentum back into p.grad, so the second half of the cascade has no code path either.)

Fix 2 (cast to fp16 before Frobenius normalization) is literally present: train/muon.py:zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 does X = G.to(dtype) and only then X = X / (X.norm() + 1e-7), and on Turing make_optimizer sets ns_dtype=torch.float16 via cuda_has_native_bf16(). But the overflow it causes in DeepSpeed cannot happen here, because Muon never sees a scaled gradient. scaler.unscale_ runs first, then clip_grad_norm_ bounds the global grad norm to 1.0, so any single matrix has Frobenius norm <= 1 and the Nesterov momentum m is at most roughly 20x that at steady state. An element near fp16's 65504 ceiling is about four orders of magnitude away. The DeepSpeed repro needed order-1 gradients times a 1e4+ loss scale, which is exactly the input this trainer has already removed.

The "silent failure" premise is also wrong for this trainer, three times over. (a) The logged loss is the true unscaled value: _micro_forward returns loss.detach().clone() taken before scaler.scale(), and loss_avg divides the all-reduced sum by loss_div*world = grad_accum, which is the exact mean even under the unequal rank_shares [82,30,78,66]. (b) rec["loss_scale"] is written on every logged step when the scaler is enabled, so a collapsing scale is visible in metrics.jsonl. (c) Most decisively, if momentum ever did go non-finite, p.add_(O, alpha=-lr) would write NaN into the weights and the NEXT step's loss would be NaN, which sets diverged (not overflow, since overflow requires a finite loss) and triggers the rollback guard, logging an {"event": "divergence"} line. The claimed end state of "zero parameter updates while the loss curve looks plausible" cannot be reached.

Two things I checked that could have changed the verdict and did not. First, configs/ultra.yaml and configs/ultra_lambda.yaml both still say optimizer: adamw, which would have made the whole candidate moot, but scripts/ultra_autostart.sh launches gui/server.py against configs/ultra_lambda_final.yaml, which scripts/ab_verdict.py generates from the A/B winner with optimizer=normuon and cautious_wd=true. NorMuon is genuinely live. Second, the tied embedding: model.py:235 aliases lm_head.weight to tok_emb.weight, and both model.parameters() and named_parameters() dedupe, so the tied tensor lands once in the AdamW group (scripts/test_train.py:179 asserts this), meaning it never reaches the Newton-Schulz path and is not double-decayed.

One true but negligible consequence remains: self.step += 1 fires on overflow steps too, so the WSD schedule advances on a step whose update was discarded. At GradScaler's default growth_interval of 2000 that is roughly 0.05% of steps in steady state. Not worth acting on.

Marking refuted because the claim's mechanism is refuted for this stack, its detection premise is refuted, and the only surviving change is a sub-0.1% precision cleanup with a nonzero restart cost.
refuted.how_to_apply:
Do the free confirmation now (no restart, about two minutes on the Lambda box, run from ~/MaxGPT/maxgpt-ultra):

1. Loss scale trend, the real health signal:
   grep -o '"loss_scale": [0-9.e+]*' runs/ultra/metrics.jsonl | tail -60
   Healthy is a high value (2^14 to 2^17) that occasionally halves and climbs back. Pinned at 128, or monotonically falling with no recovery, would be the failure. Anything else means the fp16 path is fine.

2. Divergence guard, the complete detector for poisoned optimizer state:
   grep -c '"event": "divergence"' runs/ultra/metrics.jsonl
   Zero means no NaN ever reached the weights. Non-zero means look at the surrounding lines, but note the guard already rolled back and reloaded optimizer state from the checkpoint, which restores momentum.

3. Sanity on the loss itself:
   grep -o '"loss": [0-9.]*' runs/ultra/metrics.jsonl | tail -20
   This is the true unscaled cross-entropy, so a falling curve here is real evidence, not the stale value the claim warns about.

If 1 and 2 are clean, stop. Nothing else is needed.

Optional, and only bundled into the next restart you were going to take anyway (thermal pause, the IT power cap landing, or going from 4 to 6-8 cards): reorder the normalization in train/muon.py:zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 so it normalizes in fp32 before casting. Change

    X = G.to(dtype) if dtype is not None else G
    X = X / (X.norm() + 1e-7)

to

    X = G.float()
    X = X / (X.norm() + 1e-7)
    if dtype is not None:
        X = X.to(dtype)

This does not fix an overflow here (there is none); it removes an fp16 underflow. Today the momentum matrix is cast to fp16 at its raw magnitude, where the small-element tail of a 2048x5632 matrix can land in fp16 subnormals (below 6.1e-5) and lose most of its bits before orthogonalization. Normalizing first puts every element near 3e-4, comfortably normal. Cost is one transient fp32 buffer per Muon matrix (about 46MB for the largest, freed immediately), invisible on 24GB cards. Resuming costs at most autosave_minutes = 15 minutes of compute, not the run. Do not take a dedicated restart for it.

Do not add the momentum-reorder of Fix 1. It would be a no-op against torch's GradScaler and only adds a divergence from the reference Muon implementation.

refuted.name: Checkpoint merging / EMA over the decay phase (WSM, weighted model averaging)
refuted.realistic_gain: ≈0 nats, and the single closest-scale measurement is negative: at 1.5B params / 30B tokens with uniformly shuffled data (MaxGPT-Ultra's exact regime and data ordering), EMA scored 45.29 core vs 46.21 for plain WSD decay, i.e. −0.9 points. The claimed "0.01-0.03 nats + visible downstream bump" is not supported by any source cited.
refuted.reasoning:
All three primary sources were fetched, and each fails a different way for this run.

1. WSM (arXiv:2507.17634) is measured on Ling-mini: a 16.3B-total / 1.4B-active MoE, pretrained on 10.2T tokens, with the experimental comparison run over a further 400B tokens at a 25B-token checkpoint interval. That is >10B params, MoE (an architecture family this project already rejected), and a token budget 100x this run's total. The "merge duration matters most" ablation sweeps intervals from 5B to 80B tokens: MaxGPT-Ultra's entire decay phase is 15B tokens, so the regime where that finding was established does not exist here.

2. The candidate also misstates what WSM does. The paper's method REPLACES decay: "continue training with the same constant LR. The final model is then produced by merging the checkpoints saved during this stable phase." The candidate proposes merging checkpoints taken DURING a cosine decay, which is a different operation the paper does not measure, and the benchmark deltas quoted (+3.5 MATH, +2.9 HumanEval, +5.5 MMLU-Pro) belong to merge-instead-of-decay, not merge-on-top-of-decay.

3. arXiv:2511.18903 is the only source at the right scale (1.5B / 30B tokens), and it refutes the candidate directly. Its Table 1 gives WSD+Uniform = 46.21 vs EMA+Uniform = 45.29. The authors state the effect is synergistic with an ascending-data-quality curriculum, and that "model averaging with a uniform data order under a constant learning rate does not fully match a standard WSD schedule." The headline +1.64% is curriculum vs random shuffle, not averaging vs decay. MaxGPT-Ultra's 55/23/11/8/3 mix is a uniform shuffle with no quality curriculum, so it lands squarely in the row where averaging LOSES.

4. arXiv:2306.03241 is nanoGPT 125M/335M/770M on 9B tokens (two of three under 200M) plus read-only Pythia checkpoints. Its contribution (LAWA) is faster early convergence, explicitly "quite early on during training"; it is not evidence for a final-quality gain at the end of a WSD run.

No recipe interaction actually breaks: the trainer does not wrap in DDP (`train/trainer.py:131` is a bare `model.to(device)`, gradients are hand-all-reduced), so state_dicts have no `module.` prefix; averaging fp32 master weights is orthogonal to fp16 loss scaling, and along a single trajectory NorMuon, gated attention, value residual, QK-norm and tied embeddings pose no permutation-alignment problem. The claim fails on evidence, not on mechanics.

ONE THING WORTH DOING ANYWAY, and it must happen before the decay phase begins: `configs/ultra.yaml` sets `io.keep_last_k: 3`, and `CheckpointManager._prune()` (train/checkpoint.py) deletes everything older, so at the end of the run only three checkpoints will exist and no A/B is possible even in principle. Raising `keep_last_k` (or adding a weights-only side-save) before decay costs nothing and preserves the option. Note the disk cost is not the 4.4GB quoted: `CheckpointManager.save` writes optimizer state too, so a full checkpoint at 1.1B is roughly 13-18GB, and keeping ~12 of them is ~200GB on a shared 3.3TB box. A weights-only side-save at ~4.4GB each is the right form. `keep_last` is read at CheckpointManager construction, so this takes effect at the next restart, which is already expected when IT sets the power cap and the run moves to 6-8 cards. Do not plan to ship a merged model; plan only to be able to measure one.

refuted.name: Match NorMuon's own validated 1.1B configuration (beta1 0.95, depth-scaled LR, fused QKV orthogonalization)
refuted.realistic_gain: Zero. The one actionable item (beta1 0.9 -> 0.95) is already the running value; applying it is a literal no-op, and the "brief loss bump over 200-500 steps" the candidate warns about would be self-inflicted damage for no change.
refuted.reasoning:
The paper half of the claim checks out; the codebase half is simply wrong.

VERIFIED ON THE PRIMARY SOURCE (arxiv.org/html/2510.05491v1, experimental setup): NorMuon's 1.1B/5.4B setting is indeed Muon/NorMuon beta1 = 0.95, NorMuon beta2 = 0.95, base LR 4e-4 at base depth 16 with Depth-muP (LR inversely proportional to sqrt(depth)), weight decay 0.1 on 2D hidden-layer params and 0 elsewhere, and orthogonalization applied to the concatenated QKV matrix. Trained on SlimPajama, 50B tokens, batch 2M tokens at seq 4096. The paper also lists Adam at beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.95.

REFUTATION: MaxGPT-Ultra does NOT run beta1 = 0.9 on the orthogonalized group. It already runs 0.95.
- /Users/brohm/Documents/Projects/Max's AI Model/maxgpt-ultra/train/muon.py: `def __init__(self, params, lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.1, momentum=0.95, nesterov=True, ns_steps=5, normalize=False, cautious=False, beta2=0.95, betas=(0.9, 0.95), ...)`. In this optimizer, `momentum` IS the orthogonalized group's beta1, and `betas` is used ONLY inside `_adamw_group` (the embeddings and 1D params). The candidate conflated the two.
- train/trainer.py:203 passes `"momentum": tcfg.get("muon_momentum", 0.95)`. `muon_momentum` appears nowhere else in the repo (grepped every .yaml/.py/.md, plus configs/ab/*.yaml and scripts/ab_verdict.py's FLAGS table which is what generates configs/ultra_lambda_final.yaml). So the default 0.95 is what is live.
- `beta2` is likewise never overridden, so the row-wise second moment runs at the paper's 0.95.
- `betas: [0.9, 0.95]` in configs/ultra.yaml reaches only the embedding/1D AdamW groups. That is exactly what the paper prescribes for Adam. The recipe already matches on both counts.

Two REAL deviations the candidate gestured at but got the action wrong on, neither worth acting on:
1. Weight decay on embeddings. The paper is 0 on non-2D-hidden params; train/trainer.py:50 puts the tied embedding in a group with `weight_decay=weight_decay` (0.1). This is a genuine difference from the paper, but it is also what Moonlight and essentially every GPT/Llama recipe do, the gain is unquantified and unmeasured, and flipping decay off on a ~100M-param tensor mid-run is a real perturbation for no evidence. Not a change I would make.
2. Fused QKV orthogonalization. model/model.py:97-99 has separate q_proj (2048x2048), k_proj (2048x512), v_proj (2048x512), so Newton-Schulz sees three matrices, not one 2048x3072. Genuinely different math under GQA. But the paper reports no ablation on this, it is an implementation detail rather than a measured contribution, and the candidate itself says do not touch it mid-run. Agreed. Also note it is NOT architecture-bound (an optimizer-level concat/split would do it without touching the model), so it is cheaper than "restart-class" implies, but with zero evidence of gain that is irrelevant.

On the LR: depth-muP off the paper's base gives 3.4e-4 vs the recipe's 3e-4, and the candidate concedes this is "the right neighbourhood". Worth adding that the paper's batch is 2M tokens and MaxGPT-Ultra's is 0.5M, a 4x smaller batch, which wants a LOWER LR, not a higher one. Depth-muP transfer is also only defined along the paper's width/depth ray (hidden = 128*depth, so depth 16 -> d_model 2048); MaxGPT-Ultra is d_model 2048 at 22 layers, off that ray, so the sqrt(16/22) factor is not a valid transfer anyway. And 3e-4 came out of the project's own 124M A/B. Leave it.

One thing I checked that is a non-issue: train/muon.py accumulates momentum as `buf.mul_(m).add_(g)` (Jordan convention) rather than Moonlight's `buf.lerp_(g, 1-m)`. Those differ by a constant factor 1/(1-m), which is annihilated by the `X = X / (X.norm() + 1e-7)` normalization at the top of zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 and again by the RMS-match rescale. Same direction, same magnitude. No hidden deviation there.

Note on the corroborating sources: Moonlight (2502.16982) and SOAP/Muon/Beyond (2607.20548, "SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales") both exist, but they corroborate a value the project already uses, so they add nothing actionable.
refuted.how_to_apply:
Nothing to apply. Do not touch `muon_momentum`: it is already 0.95 via the default in train/muon.py and train/trainer.py:203, and setting it "to 0.95" would change nothing while risking a fat-finger. Do not touch the LR, the QKV grouping, or the embedding weight decay mid-run.

If anything is worth doing, it is a 30-second confirmation rather than a change: on the box, `grep -n "muon_momentum\|betas\|optimizer" configs/ultra_lambda_final.yaml` should show the optimizer as `normuon` with no `muon_momentum` key, and the trainer's startup log should show the Muon group's momentum. That closes the question permanently instead of relighting it in a later sweep.

refuted.name: AdaGC: per-tensor adaptive gradient clipping
refuted.realistic_gain: Essentially zero. The paper's own closest-scale, same-optimizer cell is +0.14% zero-shot average (47.18 vs 47.04) on Llama-2 1.3B with Muon, in a setting where it explicitly reports no loss spikes occurred. The AdamW 1.3B cell is +0.01% (46.33 vs 46.32). Both are noise. Expect no measurable loss or downstream improvement at 1.1B, and zero reduction in fp16 skipped steps.
refuted.reasoning:
Refuted on three independent grounds, two of them from the paper's own text.

1. THE PAPER REFUTES IT AT THIS SCALE AND THIS OPTIMIZER. Section 5.4, quoted verbatim: "Although no loss spikes were observed under either experimental setting, AdaGC consistently demonstrated strong compatibility and generalization. In downstream zero-shot average accuracy, AdaGC outperformed GlobalGC by 0.14% (47.18% vs. 47.04%) with Muon." That is Llama-2 1.3B (essentially MaxGPT-Ultra's scale) with Muon (exactly this recipe's optimizer family), and the gain is +0.14% with nothing to fix. Table 6's Llama-2 1.3B row with AdamW: GlobalGC avg 46.32, AdaGC avg 46.33, so +0.01%. The headline +1.32% is 7B-only. Qwen3-1.7B does show +1.95%, but that is a different model family trained on 160B tokens and it directly contradicts the Llama-2 1.3B result at the same parameter count, which is the signature of a benchmark-noise-dominated regime rather than a real small-scale effect. The candidate's "+0.3-0.8% downstream and a few millinats" is an interpolation that the paper's own 1.3B rows contradict.

2. THE fp16 ARGUMENT, CALLED "THE REAL VALUE HERE," IS MECHANICALLY BACKWARDS. The claim is that per-tensor clipping "cuts the spike before it reaches the scaler." It cannot. In train/trainer.py the order is line 349 scaler.unscale_(self.optimizer), then line 350 clip_grad_norm_. torch.amp's unscale_ is what divides by the scale AND records found_inf; scaler.step() skips on that recorded flag. Clipping runs strictly afterward and cannot change it. More fundamentally, an fp16 overflow happens inside the backward pass, in the scaled gradients, before any gradient norm exists to clip against, and inf/x is still inf. AdaGC would occupy the exact same slot as the current global clip and would not prevent a single skipped step or a single scale halving. The project's own TECHNIQUES.md:337 describes this correctly. The real fp16 levers are init_scale and growth_interval, which are unrelated to AdaGC. Since the candidate concedes that on bf16 hardware this is only a nice-to-have, removing the fp16 rationale removes the case entirely.

3. NorMuon ALREADY MAKES THE UPDATE GRADIENT-MAGNITUDE-INVARIANT. train/muon.py normalizes inside Newton-Schulz (X = X / (X.norm() + 1e-7)) and then forces the final update to RMS 0.2 with O * (0.2 * sqrt(O.numel()) / (O.norm() + eps)). Scaling a tensor's gradient by h in (0,1] therefore changes the update magnitude by exactly nothing; it only perturbs the momentum buffer's mixture. Every attention and MLP matrix in the 22 layers goes through this group, so the large majority of parameters are structurally immune to what AdaGC does. That is the mechanism behind the paper's +0.14% Muon number. Only the AdamW group (tied embeddings, RMSNorm gains, the 1D attention-gate params) can be affected, and AdamW's m/sqrt(v) absorbs most of that too.

Secondary points: the paper's efficiency benefit (0.27% GPU hours at 1.3B) comes from needing only an intra-TP-group all-reduce, which does not transfer to plain DDP where every rank already holds identical all-reduced gradients and no extra collective exists to save; replacing the fused foreach clip_grad_norm_ with a per-tensor Python loop over ~200 tensors is a small net cost, not a saving. The paper never discusses mid-run adoption, so the proposed gamma warm-start is the candidate's own invention, carrying the exact silent-throttling failure mode it names, in exchange for a measured +0.14%. The recipe also already carries QK-norm, z-loss 1e-4, and 1/sqrt(depth) pre-norm scaling, three spike suppressors, and the live run has shown no spike problem to solve.

Adjacent note for the user's own question, since this investigation touched it: fp16 + fp32 master weights on Turing is a quality-neutral substitution for bf16, not a quality-losing one. Only the matmul dtype changes; master weights, optimizer state, and accumulation stay fp32, and the repo records a verification that loss-scaled and unscaled runs produce bit-identical weights (scaling by powers of two is exact). The Turing constraints cost throughput and force workarounds, not model quality.

refuted.name: More Newton-Schulz steps on the final layers only (spectral scaling laws)
refuted.realistic_gain: ~0 nats. The measured ceiling on "perfect orthogonalization" is 0.0013 nats at 124M and ~0.001 nats at 1B-4B, both within seed noise, and NorMuon's row rescale removes the mechanism entirely. At 1.1B the paper's own scaling law puts the final-O q=0.5 quantile around 1.8e-3, well clear of the 5-step failure regime.
refuted.reasoning:
Both primary sources fetched and read in full (PDFs, not just abstracts). Four independent problems, any one of which sinks it.

1) The candidate misattributes the paper's prescription. arXiv:2606.04058 Section 4 ("Case Study: Extrapolating to Frontier Scale") makes its 10-step recommendation at 300B, explicitly "a ~100x jump from our largest fitted scale of 2.8B". The concrete numbers: final O projection q=0.5 stabilizes at ~1e-3 at 2.8B with exponent -0.66, and only the extrapolation to 300B (5e-5) "falls inside the NanoGPT failure regime". At 2.8B, which is 2.5x larger than this run, 5 steps is still fine. Running the paper's own law backwards to 1.1B gives 1e-3 * (1.1/2.8)^-0.66 ~= 1.8e-3, further from the failure regime than the largest model they actually measured. The candidate's phrase "the paper's explicit prescription at ~1B" does not exist in the paper.

2) The candidate's own second source directly refutes the mechanism at exactly this scale. arXiv:2606.00371 (Hua Huang, NVIDIA) ran the ceiling experiment the spectral paper did not: an explicit FP32 SVD polar factor, i.e. the infinite-step limit of any NS schedule. On GPT-2 Small the exact SVD polar reaches final val loss 3.2809; 5-step Muon-Jordan reaches 3.2822 and 4-step Muon-Jordan reaches 3.2809, tying the exact SVD. So the entire value of going from "approximate" to "exact" is 0.0013 nats, and 5-step is very slightly worse than 4-step (noise). On 1B-4B hybrid MoE/Mamba models, a deliberately LESS accurate schedule (cubic5, 10 matmuls) matches the quintic within ~1e-3 val loss. Their stated conclusion: "training quality is not governed monotonically by polar-decomposition accuracy". If perfect orthogonalization buys nothing at 1B-4B, 10 steps buys nothing.

3) It is incoherent with NorMuon, which is what this codebase actually runs. In train/muon.py the NS output O is immediately hit with a per-row divide, O = O / (sqrt(row_v) + eps), a diagonal left-multiplication that destroys orthogonality by construction, and then a global Frobenius rescale to RMS 0.2. Paying extra matmuls to land O closer to exactly orthogonal, then multiplying it by a non-orthogonal diagonal, is spending on a property the next line discards. The row second moment O.pow(2).mean(dim=1) is also dominated by the large directions, not the small-singular-value tail the claim is about.

4) The fp16 risk argument in the candidate is backwards. zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 normalizes X = G/||G||_F first, so every value is in [0,1] and the narrow fp16 exponent range never engages (fp16 normals reach 6.1e-5, subnormals 6e-8; sigma=1e-3 squares to 1e-6, still a normal fp16 number). What matters is mantissa, and fp16 has 10 bits against bf16's 7. The cubic paper's effective lower bound l0 = 7e-3 is explicitly a bf16 artifact (< eps_bf16 = 2^-7); for fp16 the equivalent bound is ~8x lower. trainer.py:54 selects float16 on Turing, so this run has strictly MORE orthogonalization headroom than the bf16 baselines both papers studied. The Turing constraint helps here.

Minor precision note: the failure-regime figure (Figure 8) in 2606.04058 is for the NanoGPT 5-polynomial schedule b1..b5, five different polynomials. train/muon.py repeats the single quintic (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315) five times, which is the Muon-Jordan baseline of 2606.00371, the variant that tied exact SVD at 4 steps.

Cost is genuinely cheap (grad_accum is 256 on the Lambda config, so NS runs once per 256 micro-steps and is already a rounding error). The problem is not cost, it is that the gain is measured to be zero at this scale.

Scale check passes on paper (77M-2.8B brackets 1.1B), which is why this is refuted on evidence rather than on the <200M / >10B default.

WHAT THE SOURCES ACTUALLY SAY. arXiv:2607.23777, "Scale Weight Decay and Train Better" (Anuj Apte, 26 Jul 2026), is genuine and the numbers in the candidate are quoted correctly: Muon-SW replaces the (1 - lambda*eta_t) shrink factor with (1 - lambda*eta_t^2/eta_max) on matrix weights, and reaches Muon's best val loss in 264k steps vs 374k. arXiv:2512.08217 ("Correction of Decoupled Weight Decay", Chou, Dec 2025, rev Apr 2026) does independently derive the eta^2 proportionality from a steady-state weight-norm argument, so the rule itself is not junk.

THE REFUTATION IS IN THE PAPER'S OWN TEXT. It states plainly that the separation "does not arise at a fixed learning rate, where q*eta^2 and lambda*eta are both constants and the two updates coincide." That is the stable phase of WSD, verbatim. Checked against this codebase: /Users/brohm/Documents/Projects/Max's AI Model/maxgpt-ultra/train/schedule.py returns max_lr unchanged for the whole stable phase, and trainer.py:339 calls it with total_tokens 1e11 / 0.5M tokens per step = 200,000 steps, warmup_tokens 1e9 = 2,000 steps (1%), decay_frac 0.15 = 30,000 steps. So 168,000 of 200,000 steps (84%) run at eta_t = eta_max, where lambda*eta_max^2/eta_max is bit-for-bit the current update. The change is a literal no-op for the next several weeks of wall clock.

QUANTIFYING THE 16% THAT IS NOT A NO-OP. trainer.py never passes min_lr_ratio, so wsd_lr uses its 0.0 default and the cosine decays to zero, not to eta_max/10. Cumulative log-shrink difference over warmup: 2000 * lambda * eta_max * (1/2 - 1/3) = 0.010. Over the decay phase, mean(eta)/eta_max = 0.500 vs mean(eta^2)/eta_max^2 = 0.375, giving 30000 * 0.1 * 3e-4 * 0.125 = 0.113. Total ~0.12, i.e. final matrix weight norms ~12% higher, halved to ~6% by cautious weight decay's sign gate. That is a small hyperparameter nudge applied to the last 15% of training, not a convergence-speed improvement. The paper's 21-29% comes from a schedule where eta_t < eta_max for essentially 100% of steps (linear warmup of max(1000, 0.01T) then cosine straight to eta_max/10), so their whole run sits in the regime this run spends 16% of its steps in.

FOUR INDEPENDENT TRANSFER GAPS ON TOP OF THE SCHEDULE ONE.
1. Architecture mismatch: every experiment is a LLaMA-style MoE, 8 experts top-2 (72.7M-932.4M total, 30.2M-309.6M active). No dense ablation at all. MaxGPT-Ultra explicitly rejected MoE. Weight-norm stationarity in sparsely-activated expert matrices, which see a gradient on ~2/8 of steps, is exactly the setting where constant decay biases hardest, because decay applies every step while the gradient does not. A dense 1.1B does not have that pathology, so the strongest part of the paper's mechanism does not exist here.
2. Baseline decay policy mismatch: the paper trains "the embedding, un-embedding, and other non-matrix parameters with AdamW with NO weight decay." This codebase does the opposite at train/trainer.py:50, putting the tied embedding/lm_head into an AdamW group with weight_decay=0.1. With tie_embeddings: true that is the single largest matrix in the model (49152 x 2048, ~100M params, ~9% of the model) getting decay the paper's baseline never applies. The comparison being cited is against a different baseline.
3. Optimizer mismatch: the paper uses plain Muon. This run uses NorMuon (per-row second-moment renormalization, train/muon.py) plus cautious weight decay, and CWD already modifies the decay rule by gating which coordinates decay. The candidate asserts "CWD gates WHICH coordinates decay; this scales HOW MUCH, so the two compose." That is a plausible story, not a measurement. Both changes independently reduce effective decay; stacking two untested decay reductions on a run whose lambda was never tuned is a way to land at an effective lambda nobody chose.
4. Hyperparameter regime: muP with cube-root LR transfer and peak LRs of 4.8e-3 to 1.0e-2, against 3.0e-4 here, a 16-33x gap in lambda*eta per step. And ~610-650 tokens per active parameter there versus 100B/1.1B = ~91 here. Steady-state weight-norm arguments are asymptotic; the paper's runs are ~7x deeper into the asymptote.

COST AND RESTART. The candidate is right that it needs no restart and no memory. Implementation is ~3 lines, not one: train/muon.py:_muon_group reads lr and wd off the group, so eta_max has to be threaded in (trainer._set_lr at :270-272 overwrites g["lr"] every step, so a static g["max_lr"] would survive). Nothing about Turing, fp16 loss scaling, GQA, gated attention, value residual or DDP interacts with it, since the shrink is a scalar multiply on fp32 master weights. But that is the argument against doing it: the change is free, safe, AND inert. Editing the optimizer inner loop of a live multi-week DDP run to produce provably identical arithmetic for the next 84% of steps is pure downside. A typo in p.mul_(1 - ...) is silent and unrecoverable weeks later.

THE ONE CONDITIONAL WORTH REMEMBERING. If the decay phase is ever changed from cosine-to-zero to a floor (min_lr_ratio > 0, e.g. eta_max/10 as the paper uses), or if the run is restarted on a pure cosine, the rule moves from "16% of steps, ~6% weight-norm difference" toward the paper's regime and becomes worth an A/B at 124M. As the config stands today it is not. Flag it as a decay-phase decision to revisit in the same conversation where min_lr_ratio gets chosen, not as an adoption now.

refuted.reasoning:
The paper is real (arXiv:2603.10067, "HTMuon: Improving Muon via Heavy-Tailed Spectral Correction", submitted 10 Mar 2026, revised 21 May 2026) and the headline numbers in the candidate check out. Fetching the full text refutes the candidate on four independent axes.

1. THE CHEAP VARIANT ONLY BUYS A QUARTER OF THE HEADLINE GAIN. The candidate treats "HTMuon = 0.92/0.98 PPL" and "HTMuon_NS at interval 5 = net wall-clock positive" as if they were the same intervention. Table 10 says otherwise. At LLaMA-135M on 4x RTX PRO 6000: Muon 22.27 PPL in 1.40 h; HTMuon_NS(interval 5) 22.02 in 1.55 h (+10.7% time, 0.25 PPL); full HTMuon 21.24 in 6.57 h (4.7x the wall clock). The headline 0.98 PPL requires a 4.7x-wall-clock optimizer. The version that is wall-clock-positive recovers 0.25 of it, about a quarter. Same at 60M (0.34 of 0.92).

2. THE SCALE AND TOKEN-BUDGET REGIME IS WRONG FOR THIS RUN, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO ITSELF. Table 18: every LLaMA run uses seq len 256, batch 512, and the 1B model gets 90K steps / ~9-12B tokens, i.e. ~9-12 tokens per parameter. MaxGPT-Ultra is 100B tokens on 1.1B params = ~91 tokens/param (about 8x more training) at seq 2048 and ~200,000 optimizer steps. The paper's own introduction states the problem: "some studies have found that the improved performance of Muon is inversely proportional to the model scale and the number of training steps (Wen et al., 2025; Semenov et al., 2025)", and it motivates HTMuon by saying Muon's orthogonalization "may help Muon decrease the loss faster in the early phase of training". The entire mechanism is an early-phase spectral effect measured in a near-Chinchilla regime, being proposed for a 4.5x-over-Chinchilla run. The in-paper scale trend is already non-monotone (0.92 at 60M, 0.98 at 135M, 0.02 at 350M, 0.16 at 1B); the 0.02 at 350M is the paper's own strongest evidence that the effect is not scale-robust.

3. STACKING ON NORMUON COLLAPSES THE REMAINDER. The paper's stacked increments over HTMuon alone are +0.33 PPL at 60M and +0.14 at 135M, halving per scale step, and NorMuon already captures much of the same effect (the paper's own gap of HTMuon over NorMuon is 0.29 at 60M). Carrying both trends to 1B, where HTMuon over plain Muon is only 0.16 PPL on 14.33 (1.1%), the NorMuon-stacked increment lands around 0.02-0.05 PPL, ~0.15-0.35%, well under the ~1% bar. Two further configuration mismatches make even that optimistic: the paper states "we apply Muon updates to the embedding and output layers during training", which this recipe deliberately does not do (AdamW for embeddings and 1D, tied embeddings), and p=0.125 was grid-searched with no row-wise second-moment normalization in the pipeline. In train/muon.py the order would be Sigma^p, then NorMuon's per-row RMS divide, then the Moonlight 0.2-RMS rescale, and the row divide partially undoes the spectral shaping that Sigma^p just applied. Tuning p for this configuration means another 124M A/B, which is days.

4. TURING MAKES THE "LOW SINGLE-DIGIT PERCENT" COST CLAIM FALSE. The paper's own FLOP count is F = 20mnr + 4mn^2 + 6LTn^3 with L = ceil(log2(2/p)) = 4 and T = ns_steps = 5, so the extra term is 120n^3 against Muon's 20mnr: about 6x the orthogonalization FLOPs on the 2048x2048 matrices and ~2.2x on the 2048x5632 ones. Worse, HTMuon_NS computes a matrix p/2 power of M^T M by four successive Newton-Schulz square roots. Muon's quintic is fp16-stable because it only has to converge the top of the spectrum; a fractional root has to resolve the small singular values (that is the whole point of p>0), on a Gram matrix whose condition number is the square of an already heavy-tailed one. That forces fp32. Turing has no bf16 and no TF32, so fp32 on a TITAN RTX runs on CUDA cores at ~16 TFLOPS against ~110-130 TFLOPS for the fp16 tensor path the existing zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 uses (train/trainer.py sets ns_dtype to fp16 on non-bf16 cards). Roughly 3-6x the FLOPs at ~7x lower throughput is 20-40x the current NS cost. And this codebase computes the Muon update redundantly on every DDP rank (train/muon.py's docstring notes identical all-reduced grads, no sharding), so none of it is amortized across the 4-8 cards. Against a 10-33 s step at 0.5M tokens, interval 5 lands at roughly +15% to +60% wall clock, which on a 3-10 week run is weeks, not "low single-digit percent".

Restart risk is genuinely low (momentum carries over, only the map from momentum to update changes, and the trailing 0.2-RMS rescale keeps LR transfer approximately intact), with one real transient: NorMuon's row_v EMA at beta2=0.95 is estimated on O, whose row statistics shift the moment Sigma^p is inserted, so ~100 steps (~50M tokens) of mis-scaled steps. That alone would not sink it. What sinks it is a sub-0.3% expected gain, measured only in a regime 8x less trained than this run, in a paper five months old with no independent replication, paid for with a double-digit percentage of wall clock on hardware the authors never tested. Max's stated priority is zero quality loss over speed, and the correct reading of that priority here is not "take any gain at any cost", it is "do not perturb a healthy 1.1B run for a number this small and this poorly matched to the regime". Log it for the next model, where it can be A/B'd from scratch at 124M against the real recipe including NorMuon.

The A/B README (docs/ab_2026-09-21/README.md) says the live run uses configs/ultra_lambda_final.yaml, which is not in this local copy, so the Mac checkout lags the Lambda one. If the live run is not actually on NorMuon, this candidate does not apply at all.

refuted.realistic_gain: Wall clock only, and smaller than advertised: ~3-5%, not 5-15%. The candidate's own conservative recommendation (0.5M -> 1M at the midpoint) removes 25% of the optimizer steps, and optimizer steps are only ~12-19% of step wall clock (Newton-Schulz ~2-4 s replicated on every rank + an exposed ~1 s fp32 all-reduce of 4.4 GB of grads, against ~22 s of fwd/bwd at 0.5M tokens/step). 0.25 x 0.15 ~= 3.7%. refuted.reasoning:
Both primary papers are real and say roughly what the candidate says, but neither supports the specific action at this run's batch size, and the cost claim is false in this codebase.

WHAT SURVIVES (state this plainly, it answers the "are we losing quality" worry): a 2x batch ramp here is quality-neutral, and I can defend that with numbers. arXiv:2505.23971 measures CBS for a 1B model at ~4096 documents ~= 16.4M tokens (608B-token budget), and reports CBS is largely independent of model size and scales with DATA size, so at 100B tokens expect single-digit millions. arXiv:2505.02222 puts Muon's token-optimal batch at ~3.5M tokens for a 1B model on DCLM and finds Muon retains data efficiency "far beyond the so-called critical batch size", tested to 16M. MaxGPT-Ultra sits at 0.5M tokens/step: roughly 7x below Muon's token-optimal point and ~5-10x below CBS. Going to 1M stays 3-7x below. There is no token-efficiency penalty in that regime, and no interaction with the architecture: gated attention, value residual, QK-norm, GQA, 1/sqrt(depth) scaling and z-loss are all per-token forward-pass features, orthogonal to how many micro-steps you accumulate. Tied embeddings go through the AdamW group, not Muon. Memory is unaffected because micro_batch stays 1. data/loader.py keeps `pos` as an absolute global integer and deals a block of sum(shares) windows per step, so a bigger block resumes correctly with no replayed or skipped tokens. rank_shares just has to be rescaled to sum to the new grad_accum.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED FOR THIS RUN:

1. The headline evidence is about a regime this run never enters. arXiv:2602.14208 ("Fast Catch-Up, Late Switching", ICLR 2026) is a functional scaling law for SGD about WHEN to cross into the large-batch regime; the authors list untested adaptive optimizers as an explicit limitation. If you are 7x below the token-optimal batch for your optimizer the whole way, there is no threshold to time and the "late switching" content is empty. arXiv:2505.23971's OLMo-1B run starts at ~4.2M tokens and ends at ~16.8M, i.e. 8-32x above where MaxGPT sits, with Adam, sqrt LR scaling, and the same 608B token budget. Its 43%-fewer-steps figure is unreachable by a 2x ramp; a 2x ramp at the midpoint is 25%.

2. "Free... no restart, no state change" is wrong here, and the failure is silent. grad_accum is read once at Trainer construction (train/trainer.py:144) and tokens_per_step, total_steps and warmup_steps are all derived from it there (train/trainer.py:168-170). The WSD schedule is a pure function of step/total_steps (train/schedule.py, called at train/trainer.py:328). Checkpoints store `step` only, no tokens_seen (train/checkpoint.py:37-43). So a resume with grad_accum doubled restores `step` in OLD units while total_steps halves. Past 25% of the run, `while self.step < target` (train/trainer.py:401) is immediately false and training just stops. Before 25%, it silently teleports the LR curve to 2x the true progress fraction and can burn the cosine decay phase early with no error anywhere. That is a schedule-corrupting bug on a run whose stated priority is zero quality loss. There is a clean fix (halve the saved `step` on resume, since every phase boundary is token-derived; checkpoint filenames ckpt_{step:08d}.pt and latest.json would then collide/rewind), or token-index the schedule properly, but either way this is a code change to trainer.py/schedule.py/checkpoint.py plus a process restart from the last autosave, on a live run, with no test covering the resume-with-different-accum path.

3. The LR justification is a citation error, and the underlying issue is real for Muon specifically. "Muon's LR-transfer robustness (Spectral Scaling Laws, LR 0.01/0.02/0.03 at 160M)" is LR transfer across WIDTH, not across BATCH SIZE. It says nothing here. Meanwhile train/muon.py:94 rescales every update to a fixed RMS of 0.2 regardless of gradient magnitude, so total weight displacement is exactly lr x 0.2 x (number of steps). Halving the step count at fixed LR halves how far the model travels for the rest of training. That is not a no-op. Doing it correctly means the sqrt rule 2505.23971 actually used (3e-4 -> 4.24e-4), i.e. raising LR mid-run in the WSD stable phase on fp16 with dynamic loss scaling, on a trainer that aborts after 3 consecutive divergence rollbacks (train/trainer.py:407-413). That is exactly the class of change that can cost quality, which is the one thing this project said it will not trade.

4. Minor: at grad_accum 512 every fp16 overflow-skipped step (train/trainer.py:354-361) throws away 1M tokens of fwd/bwd instead of 0.5M. And momentum 0.95 with nesterov means the optimizer's smoothing window doubles in token terms (20 steps x 1M vs 20 steps x 0.5M). Both benign, both unmodelled by the cited papers.

BOTTOM LINE: the direction is right and harmless, the payoff is ~4%, and the delivery mechanism is a mid-run surgery on step accounting with a silent-corruption failure mode. Not worth it as a standalone intervention. The one thing worth carrying forward: when IT sets the power cap and the run moves to 6-8 cards, grad_accum has to change anyway (it must be a multiple of the GPU count, train/trainer.py:161-163, and rank_shares has to be re-dealt), which forces a restart-from-checkpoint and the same step-accounting fix. If the batch is ever raised, that is the free moment to do it, and the honest reason will be "we are 7x below Muon's token-optimal batch", not "late switching".

A few hours in is the cheapest moment this will ever be. If it is not done now, do not do it later in the constant phase; the bump is not worth it once the run is weeks deep.

unverified.name: Checkpoint / weight averaging over the decay window (LAWA, EMA, WSM-style merge)
unverified.claim: Running an online average of recent weights alongside training. The honest verdict from the most careful study is negative for this specific use: averaging 'acts as a proxy for a cooled-down learning rate', and its 'benefits diminish when annealing the learning rate', providing 'minimal generalization gains when a learning rate schedule already anneals to zero'. WSM, which replaces the decay with a merge entirely, reports +2.04% average over WSD (MATH 57.49→58.81, HumanEval 64.88→65.58, MMLU-Pro 53.46→56.04) but explicitly tested both 'Decay-then-Merge' and 'Merge-then-Decay' and reports both 'failed to yield any improvement'. So merging and decaying are substitutes, not complements. The remaining real value is insurance: an online EMA buffer gives a usable model at any point if the run is cut short, and averaging reaches a given target in 82% of the steps.
unverified.evidence: Ajroldi, Orvieto & Geiping, 'When, Where and Why to Average Weights?', arXiv 2502.06761 (AlgoPerf; LAWA/EMA reach target in 82% of NadamW steps, ~12% GPU-hours saved; optimal averaging window ~1% of total budget; gains collapse under LR annealing). Tian et al., WSM, arXiv 2507.17634 (16.3B total / 1.43B active MoE, 10.2T tokens, checkpoint interval 25B tokens; merge duration is the dominant factor; EMA weighting 'markedly inferior' to 1-sqrt and mean). arXiv 2511.18903 at 1.5B/30B tokens uses checkpoint averaging as a decay substitute.
unverified.estimated_gain: Approximately zero quality on top of the planned WSD cosine decay to near-zero. Do not count it as a quality lever. Real value is operational: a warm EMA copy means a school-server outage or a semester deadline during the decay does not cost the whole tail of the run.
unverified.cost: One extra fp32 copy of the 1.1B weights (~4.4GB) held on CPU, updated every N steps. Near-zero compute. Trivial to implement. Storage for a handful of decay-window checkpoints (~4.4GB each in fp32, or 2.2GB fp16 for eval-only copies).
unverified.risk: Low. The trap is believing the WSM headline and skipping the decay: that result is at 16.3B MoE on 10T tokens with a 100B-token merge duration, nothing like a 1.1B dense model on 100B tokens, and it replaces rather than augments the decay. Keep the decay.

unverified.name: Decay-phase data annealing (high-quality + instruction-formatted mix in the final 15%)
unverified.claim: Instead of holding the 55/23/11/8/3 mix constant through the cosine decay, swap the decay-phase stream for a mix that upweights math, code, curated/synthetic-textbook and instruction-formatted data, keeping a large replay fraction of the original web mix. MiniCPM's own ablation is the cleanest number: same model, same decay length, only the decay-phase data changed. 2.4B model, decay on pretrain data only (A-1) vs pretrain + high-quality/SFT data (A-2): C-Eval 40.0 -> 52.6, CMMLU 41.5 -> 51.1, MMLU 44.6 -> 50.9, GSM8K 27.7 -> 42.3, HumanEval 27.7 -> 30.4, MBPP 24.4 -> 30.3. Their 1.2B run (B-1 vs B-3): C-Eval 40.9 -> 49.1, CMMLU 41.5 -> 46.8, MMLU 47.9 -> 49.6, HumanEval 43.9 -> 44.5, MBPP 30.5 -> 32.8, GSM8K 34.2 -> 31.8 (the one regression). Crucially B-2 shows that spending the same 12B tokens as plain SFT after a pretrain-only decay gets almost nothing (C-Eval 40.9 -> 41.2), i.e. the win comes from putting that data inside the decay, not from more SFT. OLMo 2 reports +10.6 avg points (7B) and +10.3 (13B) from its 50B-token Dolmino anneal; OLMo 3 scaled that to a 100B-token Dolmino mix sampled from a 2.2T pool of math/science/code/instruction/reasoning data, selected by 10B-token 'microanneal' ablations per source then one 100B integration run. Zamba2 documents the mixing ratio that keeps this stable: ~60% replay of the original pretraining mix, ~40% new annealing data, one epoch over most sources and at most two over the best ones.
unverified.evidence: MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024) Table 1 decay-phase ablation at 1.2B and 2.4B, WSD with ~10% of tokens in decay, trillions of tokens total. OLMo 2 (Ai2, 2501.00656) 7B/13B, 50B-token anneal. OLMo 3 / Dolma 3 Dolmino (Ai2, 2512.13961), 100B-token mid-training mix built from 10B-token microanneals. Zamba2 (2411.15242) for the 60/40 replay fraction and epoch limits. SmolLM3 and IMU-1 both do the same thing (IMU-1 stage 2 tightens DCLM-edu quality threshold from >2.75 to >3.2 and Stack-edu from >3.75 to >4.1 rather than changing sources).
unverified.estimated_gain: The single largest quality lever still available on this run. Expect several points of benchmark average (MiniCPM-scale deltas of +5 to +10 on knowledge/math benchmarks are at larger token budgets and with a Chinese-heavy eval, so discount them; +2 to +5 average on MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag/GSM8K-style evals at 1.1B/100B is the honest band). Costs zero extra tokens: it is a reweighting of the ~15B tokens already budgeted for decay.
unverified.cost: Implementation: a second dataloader mix config plus a switch at the decay step. No architecture or optimizer change, no restart. Compute: zero extra. Main work is preparing the high-quality shard now, while the stable phase runs: tokenize the extra math/code/instruction sources (OpenWebMath is already in the mix and can be upweighted; add FineMath-4+, Stack-edu or MegaMath, and a chat-formatted slice of UltraChat/OASST) into the same 49,152-vocab BPE. On Turing this is CPU-side work and does not touch the GPUs.
unverified.risk: Two real risks. (1) Repetition: the high-quality pool must be big enough that the decay sees it at most ~2 epochs; below that, measured returns fall off past ~4 repetitions. (2) Overfitting the eval: adding instruction-formatted data to pretraining makes the base model look better on few-shot benchmarks partly because it has seen the format. MiniCPM's GSM8K regression at 1.2B (34.2 -> 31.8) is a reminder this is not free on every task. Mitigation: keep the 60/40 replay, hold out a clean validation slice of the original mix, and check that held-out loss on the ORIGINAL mix does not blow up during decay.

unverified.name: Checkpoint averaging / merging at the end of the decay (WSM, PMA, EMA)
unverified.claim: Average the last N saved checkpoints instead of shipping the single final one. Three independent 2025-2026 lines agree it is a free win and that it is, formally, a substitute for LR decay. WSM (Warmup-Stable-Merge) shows the equivalence between LR decay and checkpoint merging and beats a tuned WSD decay baseline by +2.04% average (MATH +2.30, HumanEval +1.08, MMLU-Pro +4.83) on a 16.3B-total/1.43B-active MoE trained on 10.2T tokens with a 400B-token comparison phase; it finds merge DURATION (the token span the window covers) matters more than checkpoint interval or count, uses 25B-token intervals, and says n=12 recent checkpoints is enough for an online sliding window. Their weighting ablation: 1-sqrt weights 64.06 avg vs simple mean 63.95, and EMA worst. PMA (ByteDance Seed) tested dense 411M to 70B and MoE 0.7B/7B to 20B/200B and recommends N=10 checkpoints with simple moving average, with the interval scaling with model size (~8B tokens for a 1.3B/13B-class model at a ~200B budget); merging during the STABLE phase already matches or beats the annealed checkpoint, so it also gives you a free preview of annealed quality before you spend the decay. IMU-1, the closest match to this project, applies post-hoc EMA with beta=0.8 over the final 10 checkpoints and reports +0.014 average benchmark on top of everything else at 430M / 72B tokens.
unverified.evidence: WSM (2507.17634), Ling-mini 16.3B MoE, 10.2T + 400B tokens, Tables 1-3. PMA (2505.12082), dense 411M-70B and MoE, e.g. Seed-Dense-70B HumanEval 50.6 -> 57.9, GSM8K 85.9 -> 91.3 after merging. IMU-1 (2602.02522), 430M dense, 72B tokens, EMA beta=0.8 over last 10 ckpts, +0.014 avg. LAWA line of work: an averaging window around 1% of the total training budget is consistently near-optimal and is stable to the exact choice.
unverified.estimated_gain: +0.5 to +2 points of benchmark average, for literally zero extra training compute. The most reliable small win on this list.
unverified.cost: Implementation: a checkpoint-averaging script (load N state_dicts on CPU, weighted mean of fp32 master weights, save). Compute: none. Disk: N x ~4.4GB fp32 (or save bf16... not available on Turing, so fp16 or fp32 copies). At 0.5M tokens/step and 100B tokens = 200k steps, a 1B-token interval is every 2000 steps; keep a rolling window of 10-12. On the Lambda box with no root, check the scratch quota first: 12 x 4.4GB fp32 weights-only is ~53GB, which is fine if optimizer state is not also saved for every window checkpoint (save weights-only for the merge window).
unverified.risk: Low. Two caveats: (1) average the WEIGHTS only, from checkpoints spaced far enough apart that they are not the same point (WSM found short merge durations underperform); (2) do not average across the data-mix switch at the start of the decay if the mix change is large. Concretely: run the window entirely inside the decay phase, or entirely inside the stable phase, not straddling. Validate the merged model on held-out loss before declaring it the final model, because merging can occasionally be neutral rather than positive.

unverified.name: Lengthen decay to ~20% of tokens and use a 1-sqrt (or exponential) shape instead of cosine
unverified.claim: The planned 15% cosine decay is inside the defensible band but is not the shape the WSD literature converged on. MiniCPM found 10% of steps sufficient and 2.5% clearly too short, and used EXPONENTIAL annealing with T=5000 steps (20B tokens); independent replications report final loss is essentially flat for decay fractions between 8% and 12%. IMU-1's ablation is the most directly comparable: WSD with a 20% decay using a 1-sqrt profile matches a full cosine schedule while keeping the pre-decay checkpoint reusable, whereas 10% decay leaves the model undertrained; they also report inverse-sqrt base + 20% decay beating constant + 40% decay. WSM's weighting ablation independently favours the 1-sqrt profile (64.06 vs 63.95 for linear/mean).
unverified.evidence: MiniCPM (2404.06395): '10% steps are enough', 2.5% insufficient, exponential anneal T=20B tokens. IMU-1 (2602.02522): WSD + 20% decay with 1-sqrt matches cosine at 430M/72B tokens. WSM (2507.17634) Table 3: 1-sqrt > mean. Community replications (marin-community/marin issue #764) report 8-12% decay fractions perform within noise of each other.
unverified.estimated_gain: Small and honest: on the order of 0.005-0.015 nats of held-out loss, mostly from the shape rather than the length. The real value is optionality: a 1-sqrt profile puts more of the decay early, so an intermediate decayed checkpoint is usable sooner.
unverified.cost: One line in the LR scheduler. Zero compute. Can be changed at any point before the decay starts.
unverified.risk: Effectively none, as long as the change is made BEFORE the decay begins (changing the LR shape mid-decay is a discontinuity). Going longer than ~30% decay shows diminishing and possibly negative returns, so do not exceed 20-25%. Note the tension with the curriculum candidate below, which argues for a HIGHER ending LR: pick one, do not average the two recommendations.

unverified.name: Quality-ascending data ordering for remaining stable-phase tokens (+ moderate ending LR, + curriculum model averaging)
unverified.claim: Order the remaining pretraining stream by a quality score (DCLM fastText or PreSelect), lowest quality first, highest quality last, so the highest-quality documents land where the model can still learn from them. The paper's framing is that standard aggressive LR decay 'wastes your best data': a quality-ascending curriculum substantially beats random shuffling under a CONSTANT LR, and that advantage is largely destroyed by decaying to near-zero. Their fix is either (a) decay only moderately, ending at ~1/3 of peak LR (1e-3 from a 3e-3 peak) instead of ~1e-5, or (b) replace the decay entirely with weighted averaging of final checkpoints (they call it CMA: constant LR + EMA alpha=0.2 over the last 6 checkpoints). Combined, they report +1.64% average benchmark over random shuffle + standard decay at 1.5B parameters / 30B tokens, and 1.2-2.2% improvements on core benchmarks in their mid-training setting, with no additional data refinement.
unverified.evidence: 'How Learning Rate Decay Wastes Your Best Data' (2511.18903), Qwen2.5-1.5B architecture, 30B tokens, quality scored with DCLM fastText and PreSelect, Tables 1-2.
unverified.estimated_gain: +1 to +1.6% average benchmark if the full recipe is adopted. But the effect is entangled with candidate 1: if the decay phase is already being annealed on a hand-picked high-quality mix, the curriculum is doing much the same job and the gains will not simply add. The defensible partial adoption is the ORDERING alone (free, no LR change).
unverified.cost: Implementation: score the untokenized remainder of the corpus with the DCLM fastText classifier (CPU, hours for tens of billions of tokens) and re-shard the remaining tokenized data in ascending score order. Zero GPU cost. Must be done before the tokens are consumed.
unverified.risk: Moderate, and this is the one to be skeptical about. Two specific concerns. (1) The 'end at 1/3 of peak LR' recommendation directly contradicts the MiniCPM/OLMo decay-to-near-zero practice that candidate 1 depends on, and their evidence is a single 1.5B / 30B-token study, one third the token budget here. Do NOT adopt the moderate-ending-LR part without adopting their averaging replacement too, or you get the worst of both. (2) Sorting by quality means the model spends a long stretch on the lowest-quality documents; at 100B tokens that is a much longer degraded stretch than in a 30B-token run, and nobody has measured it at that horizon. Safe version: mild ascending ordering (bucket the remainder into 3-4 quality tiers rather than a strict sort), keep the planned decay to near-zero, and take the checkpoint averaging from candidate 2.

unverified.name: Swap remaining FineWeb-Edu stream for Ultra-FineWeb-en
unverified.claim: Ultra-FineWeb applies a verified fastText filter (dim 256, 3-gram, 3 epochs) on top of FineWeb, with the classifier's training data validated by a two-stage annealing probe on an almost-trained 1B model rather than by from-scratch runs. Measured English average: Ultra-FineWeb-en 45.891 vs FineWeb-Edu 44.560 (+1.33 points) vs FineWeb 42.287 (+3.60 points). ~1T English tokens released, so there is plenty for the ~50B tokens left in the 55% web slice.
unverified.evidence: Ultra-FineWeb (2505.05427, OpenBMB), English benchmark average across the standard suite; verification protocol uses a ~1B model with two-stage annealing, which is exactly this project's scale.
unverified.estimated_gain: +0.5 to +1.3 points of English benchmark average on the portion of the run that still uses it. Because only roughly half the web tokens remain, halve the headline number: realistically +0.3 to +0.7 overall.
unverified.cost: Tokenize the new shards with the existing 49,152 BPE (CPU work, can overlap with training) and point the web slice at the new files at a shard boundary. No GPU cost, no restart. Free download from HuggingFace.
unverified.risk: Two things to check before switching. (1) Overlap: Ultra-FineWeb-en is filtered from FineWeb, and FineWeb-Edu is also from FineWeb, so some documents already seen will reappear. At these volumes a small overlap is harmless (repetitions up to ~4x are about as good as fresh data) but do not let it become a large fraction. (2) Distribution shift at the switch point can cause a visible loss bump for a few hundred steps; this is cosmetic if the mix proportions are kept identical. Honest caveat: a +1.3 point delta measured by the dataset's own authors on their own filter is the weakest kind of evidence on this list.

unverified.name: Post-hoc rank-1 extrapolation of the merged checkpoints (Extra-Merge)
unverified.claim: Late in training, averaged checkpoints collapse onto an approximately one-dimensional linear manifold. Extra-Merge runs PCA over K=4 merged checkpoints to find that direction and then extrapolates along it with a 1-D line search on a validation set (~11 candidate step sizes). Completely training-free: no gradients, no extra tokens. Reports consistent validation-loss reduction over both raw baselines and standard checkpoint merging in pretraining, and +0.59% average accuracy over the raw baseline on Pythia-12B across ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and PIQA. Explicitly verified to work with Muon as well as AdamW, which matters here because the run uses NorMuon.
unverified.evidence: Extra-Merge (2605.26484): GPT-2 124M/355M/1.55B on 10B FineWeb tokens, LLaMA 0.5B and 2B on C4, plus post-hoc on public Pythia-12B checkpoints. Works with AdamW and Muon.
unverified.estimated_gain: +0.3 to +0.6% average accuracy on top of plain checkpoint averaging. Small, but the marginal cost over candidate 2 is one afternoon of scripting and a handful of eval passes.
unverified.cost: Requires the checkpoints from candidate 2 to already exist. Then: PCA over 4 merged weight vectors (CPU, minutes) plus ~11 validation evaluations of a 1.1B model, which is a few GPU-minutes each. No training.
unverified.risk: Low but real: the line search is fit on a validation set, so with a small or unrepresentative validation set you can pick a step size that overfits it. Use a held-out slice not drawn from the anneal mix, and verify the chosen extrapolation also improves a second, independent held-out set before shipping. If neither improves, take the plain average and move on.

unverified.name: Best-fit packing (eliminate document truncation in sequence packing)
unverified.claim: Naive concatenate-then-chunk packing truncates a large fraction of documents mid-sentence, and those fragments teach the model to state ungrounded continuations. Best-fit packing solves a length-aware bin-packing problem so documents are packed without unnecessary truncation, at the same sequence utilisation. Reported relative improvements: reading comprehension +4.7%, context following +16.8%, program synthesis +9.2%, and up to 58.3% reduction in closed-domain hallucination.
unverified.evidence: 'Fewer Truncations Improve Language Modeling' (2404.10830), ICML 2024, LM pretraining on text and code. Caveat stated plainly: the abstract does not give model sizes or token counts and I did not extract them from the body (the PDF fetch returned binary), so the scale behind those percentages is unverified here.
unverified.estimated_gain: Modest for loss, potentially meaningful for code and for factual grounding. Applies only to the ~half of the run still ahead, so halve whatever you expect. The program-synthesis number is the one most relevant to the 11% CodeParrot slice.
unverified.cost: A data-pipeline change only: re-pack the remaining tokenized shards with a best-fit-decreasing bin packer instead of the current concatenation. CPU-only, no GPU cost, no restart, no change to the model or optimizer. If documents are already concatenated into a flat token stream on disk, this requires having kept document boundaries; if boundaries were discarded at tokenization, this one is unavailable without re-tokenizing.
unverified.risk: Low. Mid-run change in the packing distribution is benign (the model sees the same tokens, differently grouped). The practical blocker is whether document boundary offsets were preserved. Note this pairs with, and is partly subsumed by, intra-document masking below: if you do document masking, truncation still hurts, so best-fit packing remains worth it either way, and it is the cheaper of the two on Turing.

unverified.name: Intra-document attention masking (block cross-document attention within packed sequences)
unverified.claim: With standard causal masking over packed sequences, tokens attend across document boundaries to unrelated text. Masking attention to stay within each document removes that distraction. Measured: intra-doc masking reaches 44.48% average downstream vs 43.38% for standard causal masking. The same line of work shows that choosing WHICH documents get packed together matters too: retrieval-based sequence construction gives +11.6% in-context learning, +9.8% knowledge memorisation. Reported implementation cost in a FlashAttention-2 setting is about a 4% pretraining slowdown.
unverified.evidence: 'Analysing The Impact of Sequence Composition on Language Model Pre-Training' (2402.13991); corroborated by later comparative studies and the llm.c discussion thread on cross-document contamination.
unverified.estimated_gain: About +1 point of downstream average if applied for a whole run. Applied to only the remaining ~half of this run, expect roughly +0.3 to +0.5, and possibly less because the model has already learned to ignore cross-document context.
unverified.cost: This is the one where the Turing constraint bites. The quoted 4% overhead assumes FlashAttention-2's varlen path, which does not exist on sm_75. Options here are torch SDPA's memory-efficient backend with an explicit block-diagonal attn_mask (materialises a 2048x2048 mask per sequence, real memory and bandwidth cost on 24GB cards) or FlexAttention (Triton-based, sm_75 support is not reliable). Realistic slowdown on these cards: 10-30%, not 4%. At 3-10 weeks projected wall clock, a 20% slowdown costs days.
unverified.risk: Moderate, and my honest read is SKIP this one mid-run. The gain is the smallest of the data-pipeline candidates and the cost is the largest on this specific hardware, plus a mid-run change to the attention mask is a genuine (if mild) train/test distribution shift the model has to re-adapt to. If it is adopted at all, adopt it only for the decay phase, where the high-quality documents are the ones you most want uncontaminated, and measure the actual tokens/s on one node before committing.

unverified.name: Mid-training context extension from 2048 to 4096/8192
unverified.claim: Standard modern practice is to pretrain short and extend context in a dedicated mid-training stage: raise the RoPE base frequency, upsample long documents, train for a comparatively small number of tokens. SmolLM3 spent 100B extra tokens extending beyond its 4K window; K2-V2 uses four stages (8K/64K/128K/512K with RoPE base 0.5M/1M/10M/10M); Cerebras extended Llama3-8B-Instruct to 16K-32K with under 10B tokens, about 80x less than the original recipe, using synthetic long-context data, RoPE position-ID shifting and a raised base frequency. SkyLadder separately argues short-context pretraining followed by expansion beats a fixed long context on both throughput and downstream quality, which retroactively validates the seq-2048 choice here.
unverified.evidence: SmolLM3 (HuggingFace, 2025) 100B-token long-context mid-training; K2-V2 (2512.06201) staged RoPE base schedule; Cerebras context-extension blog (<10B tokens for an 8B model); SkyLadder (2503.15450) context-window scheduling, ~1B-7B models on SlimPajama.
unverified.estimated_gain: Zero on short-context quality. Purely a capability add: it lets the finished chat model handle prompts longer than 2048 tokens. If the deliverable is a chat demo with normal-length turns, the gain is nil.
unverified.cost: Several billion tokens of extra training at 4096 or 8192 sequence length, which on Turing fp16 with no FlashAttention means attention memory scaling quadratically: at 8192 the attention matrices are 16x the 2048 case, which likely will not fit at the current batch size on 24GB and would force gradient accumulation with a smaller micro-batch. Realistically 1-2 extra weeks on this cluster.
unverified.risk: My recommendation is DEFER. It is the only candidate here that costs a large number of extra tokens for zero gain on the evaluation the project actually cares about, and the SFT/DPO data (UltraChat, OASST, UltraFeedback) is overwhelmingly short. If long context is wanted later, it can be done as a genuinely separate stage after post-training without touching this run. Do NOT attempt it by simply raising the RoPE base without any training: that degrades short-context quality.

unverified.name: Principled annealing-sample selection (DiReCT / Hessian-spectrum selection)
unverified.claim: Rather than hand-picking the anneal mix by source, select individual samples whose gradients align with low-curvature eigendirections of the validation Hessian while bounded in the high-curvature subspace. Measured at exactly this project's scale: Llama-1.1B on The Pile with a ~1.8M-sample (2.1GB) annealing pool spanning math, code and long-context, ~2 percentage points aggregate benchmark improvement over uniform sampling, with 3.4-5.0 point gains on GSM8K and HumanEval specifically. Also validated at GPT-2-Medium 355M on SlimPajama.
unverified.evidence: DiReCT (2605.31175), GPT-2-Medium 355M / SlimPajama and Llama-1.1B / The Pile, annealing pool ~1.8M samples.
unverified.estimated_gain: Claimed ~2pp aggregate over uniform sampling of the same pool. But note the baseline is UNIFORM sampling, not a well-chosen source mix; against a MiniCPM/Dolmino-style hand mix (candidate 1) the marginal gain is unmeasured and probably much smaller.
unverified.cost: A full forward pass over the annealing pool to gather per-sample gradient projections, randomized sketching to approximate the Hessian, then a successive-convex-approximation solve (max 20 iterations). The authors themselves concede gradient gathering over the full training set is 'nontrivial'. On 4 Turing cards, with the pretraining run occupying them, this is days of contended compute plus a nontrivial amount of novel code.
unverified.risk: My recommendation is SKIP. The evidence is a single 2026 paper, the gain is measured against a weak baseline, and the implementation is the most complex item on this list for a solo high-school project with no root on the box. Candidate 1 captures most of the same effect (upweight math/code/instruction in the decay) with a config change instead of a research implementation. Listed here so the decision is explicit rather than an oversight.

unverified.name: Post-hoc checkpoint EMA / weight averaging over the decay phase
unverified.claim: Instead of shipping the last iterate, average the final N decay-phase checkpoints (EMA with beta≈0.8 over the last 10 checkpoints, saved every ~5k steps). IMU-1 measured avg benchmark 0.560 -> 0.574 (+0.014) at 430M, with HellaSwag 0.503->0.511 and LAMBADA 0.482->0.513. WSM (the general theory: LR decay IS model averaging) reports +2.04% avg on the base model over a tuned WSD baseline, +3.5 MATH / +2.9 HumanEval / +5.5 MMLU-Pro, and finds merge DURATION (how wide the averaging window is) matters more than checkpoint interval or count. The Kempner 'Anytime Pretraining' work shows EMA-averaged constant/1-over-sqrt-t schedules track the cosine envelope at every horizon from 1x to 32x Chinchilla.
unverified.evidence: IMU-1 (arXiv 2602.02522), 430M dense on 72B tokens, the paper Max's value-residual + NorMuon + cautious-WD recipe came from, measured on a 6-benchmark average. WSM (arXiv 2507.17634, ICLR 2026) on Ling-mini 16.3B-A1.4B MoE, +400B tokens from a 10.2T checkpoint, AdamW, ckpt every 25B tokens. Anytime Pretraining (arXiv 2602.03702, Kempner) at 150M and 300M dense, 3.3B-105.6B tokens, multiple simultaneous EMAs at half-life fractions f in {0, 6.25, 12.5, 25, 50, 100}% of elapsed time.
unverified.estimated_gain: +0.01 to +0.015 absolute on a benchmark average (roughly a 1-2% relative accuracy gain) for a 1.1B on 100B tokens. This is the single best-evidenced free lunch on the list: it is measured at 430M with an almost identical recipe.
unverified.cost: Zero training compute. Just save checkpoints every ~5k steps through the decay phase (he already checkpoints) and run a weighted average on CPU at the end. ~4.4GB fp32 per checkpoint, ~50GB of disk for 10. Implementation is ~20 lines. Do the averaging in fp32 on CPU, not on the Turings.
unverified.risk: Very low. It is post-hoc: keep both the last iterate and the averaged weights and evaluate both. If the average is worse, throw it away. Only real risk is disk quota on a school box with no root.

unverified.name: Lengthen the decay to 20% of tokens and use 1-sqrt shape, not cosine
unverified.claim: IMU-1 ablated the WSD decay fraction directly: 20% decay matches a tuned cosine exactly (3.125 train loss both), 10% decay is +3.5% relative loss (badly undertrained), and 30% decay is +1.5% worse. The current plan decays over the last 15%, which sits between the sweet spot and the known-bad short decay. IMU-1 also uses a 1-sqrt decay shape rather than cosine, and the ablation literature on annealing functions finds 1-sqrt the best of the tested cooldown shapes; WSM independently derives 1-sqrt-decay-equivalent merge weights from its theory.
unverified.evidence: IMU-1 (arXiv 2602.02522) decay-fraction ablation at 70M proxy scale, then applied at 430M/72B with a 1-sqrt decay in both stage 2 and stage 3. WSM (arXiv 2507.17634) Theorem 3.1 derives merge weights that emulate 1-sqrt decay and uses it as its reference schedule. Anytime Pretraining (arXiv 2602.03702) at 150M/300M shows 1/sqrt(t) schedules match cosine within noise across 1x-32x Chinchilla.
unverified.estimated_gain: Small but real: avoiding the short-decay regime is worth low single-digit percent relative loss. The decay-fraction ablation is at 70M so treat the exact 20% number as a guide, not a law. The 1-sqrt vs cosine swap is close to free and at worst neutral.
unverified.cost: Zero. Both are scheduler changes that take effect when the decay starts, which has not started. One config edit.
unverified.risk: Low. Going 15% -> 20% spends 5B more tokens in decay, so the constant phase gets 5B shorter at fixed 100B budget. If he would rather not shorten the stable phase he can extend total tokens instead. The 70M ablation scale is the main caveat: the optimal fraction may shift at 1.1B.

unverified.name: Fine-grained WSD: add a high-quality stable sub-phase before the decay
unverified.claim: Split the constant-LR phase into a 'diversity-enriched stable' part (current mix) and a later 'high-quality stable' part (tighter quality filters, more Cosmopedia/math/code, less raw web) at the SAME peak LR, and only then decay. Nanbeige ablated exactly this at 1B on 1T tokens against vanilla WSD: GSM8k 27.1 -> 34.3 (+7.2), CMATH 34.5 -> 39.5 (+5.0), BBH 29.3 -> 31.6 (+2.3), MMLU 49.2 -> 50.6 (+1.4), CMMLU 50.3 -> 51.9 (+1.6), MMLU-Pro 16.87 -> 18.64 (+1.77). IMU-1 does the same thing under a different name: DCLM-edu threshold >2.75 in stage 1, >3.2 in stage 2, dropped entirely in stage 3.
unverified.evidence: Nanbeige4-3B technical report (arXiv 2512.06266), FG-WSD ablation run at 1B parameters / 1T tokens, direct A/B against vanilla WSD. Production run used 0.1T warmup / 12.4T diversity-stable / 6.5T high-quality-stable / 4T decay. IMU-1 (arXiv 2602.02522) three-stage schedule with per-stage quality thresholds, 29B/28B/14B tokens at 430M.
unverified.estimated_gain: The +7.2 GSM8k is at 1B but on 1T tokens, 10x Max's budget, so scale it down. Realistically +1 to +3 points on math/reasoning benchmarks and ~+1 on MMLU for a 1.1B/100B run. This is the biggest measured downstream gain of anything here that costs nothing.
unverified.cost: Zero compute. It is a data-loader change: re-shard the remaining stream with a tighter FineWeb-Edu score threshold and a higher Cosmopedia/OpenWebMath/code share for the last ~20-25B tokens of the constant phase. A few hours of data prep on CPU while training continues.
unverified.risk: Low to moderate. Changing the mix mid-run introduces a distribution shift at a constant LR, which can produce a visible loss bump for a few hundred steps. Ramp the mix over ~1B tokens rather than switching in one step. Also make sure the new shards are disjoint from what has already been consumed, or the 100B 'unique tokens' claim quietly becomes false.

unverified.name: Decay-phase annealing mix: synthetic reasoning (SYNTH) + instruction-formatted data
unverified.claim: Every 2026 small-model recipe puts synthetic reasoning traces and instruction-formatted data into the annealing/mid-training mix, not just cleaner web. IMU-1's stage 2/3 add PleIAs SYNTH (4.8B then 1.0B tokens) plus Cosmopedia-edu and MegaMath and drop raw web entirely by stage 3; that is the main reason a 430M on 72B tokens 'approaches models trained on 56x more data'. Olmo 3's Dolmino mid-training mix is 100B tokens sampled from a 2.2T pool of math/science/code/instruction-following/reading-comprehension plus reasoning traces, chosen by micro-annealing experiments. SYNTH itself is free and open: 79.6M samples, ~75B tokens, explicitly built so small models converge to SOTA in ~100B tokens.
unverified.evidence: IMU-1 (arXiv 2602.02522) per-stage data tables at 430M/72B. PleIAs SYNTH dataset card (HF) and Baguettotron, a 321M model trained only on SYNTH for 200B tokens, reported best-in-class in its size range. Olmo 3 (arXiv 2512.13961, Ai2 blog) Dolma 3 Dolmino: 100B-token mid-training mix from a 2.2T pool, built by 'micro-annealing' each candidate source then integration-testing the combination.
unverified.estimated_gain: Hard to bound, this is where most of IMU-1's sample-efficiency claim lives. Plausibly the largest quality lever still available without a restart, especially on reasoning/math evals. Expect several points on GSM8k-class tasks if the decay mix gets 20-40% synthetic reasoning + instruction data.
unverified.cost: Free data, CC-permissive. ~75B tokens of SYNTH is a large download and needs retokenizing with his 49,152 byte-level BPE. Budget a day of CPU-side prep; it can run while the GPUs train. No change to the training loop.
unverified.risk: Moderate and worth stating plainly: heavy synthetic-reasoning data in the decay phase makes the base model look much better on benchmarks and can make it more benchmark-shaped. It also partially overlaps with what SFT is supposed to do. Keep the decay mix at most ~40% synthetic and keep a held-out non-synthetic loss track so the improvement is not purely eval-flavored.

unverified.name: Do not bury the best data under a near-zero learning rate
unverified.claim: The standard 'save the best data for last' instinct fights the LR schedule: data seen when the LR has decayed to near zero barely moves the weights. The recommendation from a direct study is to place the highest-quality data where the LR is still around 1/3 of peak, use a MORE MODERATE decay than you would for uniform data, and recover the rest of the decay benefit with model averaging instead. Measured at 1.5B on 30B tokens (DCLM 1B-1x): CMA (constant LR + averaging of final checkpoints) is +0.8% on core benchmarks over the standard baseline; in the mid-training scenario +1.2% average and >2% on core; combined CDMA (moderate decay + averaging + curriculum ordering) is +1.64% average over random shuffling.
unverified.evidence: 'How Learning Rate Decay Wastes Your Best Data in Curriculum-Based LLM Pretraining' (arXiv 2511.18903), 1.5B parameters / 30B tokens on DCLM-LM. This is the closest published scale to Max's run of anything in this sweep. Consistent with WSM's finding that averaging can substitute for decay entirely.
unverified.estimated_gain: +1 to +1.6% average benchmark accuracy, measured at 1.5B/30B. This composes with candidates 1 and 3 rather than duplicating them: it is the instruction on WHERE in the schedule the good data goes.
unverified.cost: Zero. It is a sequencing decision about the decay phase, which has not started.
unverified.risk: Low, but it is in mild tension with the FG-WSD candidate. The resolution the papers point at: put the high-quality stable sub-phase at full LR (candidate 3), start the decay with that mix already in place, and rely on checkpoint averaging (candidate 1) rather than a very deep final decay. Do not put a brand-new best-data source into the last 2% of the run.

unverified.name: Nemotron-CC-HQ instead of more FineWeb-Edu for the remaining web fraction
unverified.claim: FineWeb-Edu gets its quality by an aggressive model-based filter that discards ~90% of data, which costs diversity. Nemotron-CC relaxes the heuristic filters, ensembles a FineWeb-Edu-style classifier with a DCLM classifier, and adds synthetic rephrasing to recover diversity. Its high-quality subset beats FineWeb-Edu on most tasks, and Nemotron-CC-HQ improves MMLU by 5.6 points over DCLM at 8B/1T tokens, with 4x more unique real tokens than DCLM at full scale.
unverified.evidence: Nemotron-CC (arXiv 2412.02595, ACL 2025). The +5.6 MMLU number is at 8B parameters / 1T tokens, so it is far above Max's scale and should be discounted accordingly. The diversity argument matters more at 100B unique tokens than the headline number does.
unverified.estimated_gain: Modest at 1.1B/100B, maybe +0.5 to +1.5 MMLU if it replaces a meaningful share of the remaining web tokens. Its real value is as the web component of the high-quality-stable and decay mixes rather than as a wholesale swap.
unverified.cost: Free, open dataset. Download plus retokenization. Does not touch the training loop.
unverified.risk: Low on quality, moderate on logistics. Swapping the base web source for the whole run is effectively a restart of the data pipeline and is not worth it a few hours in; restrict this to the remaining mix. Nemotron-CC contains synthetic rephrased text, so it stacks with candidate 4's synthetic share: count them together against the 'how synthetic is this model' budget.

unverified.name: Adaptive gradient clipping (AdaGC per-tensor EMA, or ZClip z-score) replacing the fixed clip=1.0
