unverified.claim: Replace the global fixed-norm clip with a per-tensor threshold set from an EMA of that tensor's own historical clipped norms (AdaGC) or a z-score test on the global-norm history (ZClip). AdaGC drives the reported 'spike score' to exactly 0 on every model tested and improves downstream accuracy over global clipping by +1.32% (Llama-2 7B), +1.27% (Mixtral 8x1B) and +2.48% (ERNIE 10B-A1.4B). The stated mechanism is the one that matters on fp16: a single outlier gradient that survives a fixed clip contaminates the optimizer's momentum state for thousands of steps, so the trigger (a bad doc, an fp16 overflow, a bit flip) matters less than stopping it before it reaches the moving averages.
unverified.evidence: AdaGC (arXiv 2502.11034, ICML 2026 poster) on Llama-2 7B, Mixtral 8x1B, ERNIE 10B-A1.4B; explicitly reported as optimizer-agnostic and tested with Muon and Lion. ZClip (arXiv 2504.02507) is the simpler z-score variant, same family. AGGC (arXiv 2601.11864) is the group-wise variant.
unverified.estimated_gain: Close to 0 expected loss gain on a run that never spikes; the real value is insurance. At 1.1B/100B on 24GB Turing fp16 with dynamic loss scaling, a spike that poisons NorMuon's momentum is one of the few things that can silently cost weeks, and this is the cheapest known guard. Treat the +1.3-2.5% downstream numbers as an upper bound measured at 7-10B where instability was actually occurring.
unverified.cost: ~30 lines: keep one scalar EMA per parameter tensor (negligible memory, no extra allreduce; it is cheaper than global clipping in DDP because it is local). No restart. Must be applied AFTER GradScaler.unscale_ and before the NorMuon/AdamW step; on the first ~100 steps fall back to the fixed clip while the EMA warms up.
unverified.risk: Changing the clipping rule mid-run changes the update distribution slightly, so the loss curve will have a small discontinuity even if nothing is wrong. Per-tensor clipping interacts with Newton-Schulz: NorMuon's orthogonalization is already scale-invariant per matrix, so per-tensor clipping mostly affects the AdamW (embedding/1D) group and the momentum buffers. Do not also keep a tight global clip on top, or you double-clip.

unverified.name: fp16 cast policy from the Kaiyuan-2B recipe: fp32 softmax and RMSNorm, plus activation/logit max telemetry
unverified.claim: The only recent technical report of a ~2B dense model actually pretrained in fp16 on pre-Ampere hardware (Ascend 910A, explicitly described as V100-class) states its precision policy as: FP32 for Softmax and RMSNorm, FP16 for everything else. It also gives the concrete failure curve: maximum activation values exceeded 10,000 after one trillion tokens, 'close to the FP16 upper limit' (65504), and it localises instability to exactly two places, the attention logits and the post-SwiGLU MLP activations.
unverified.evidence: PCMind-2.1-Kaiyuan-2B Technical Report (arXiv 2512.07612), 2B params / 1.4B non-embedding, Ascend 910A clusters, fp16 throughout. Same two hot spots are confirmed independently by the small-scale-proxies line of work (arXiv 2309.14322) which reproduces attention-logit growth at small scale under large LR.
unverified.estimated_gain: No loss improvement by itself. It converts a class of run-ending fp16 overflows into a non-event. The 10,000-at-1T-tokens number scales roughly with tokens seen, so at 100B tokens the headroom is real but shrinking, and the value residual (layer-1 values injected into every layer) is a new path for activation magnitude to accumulate that none of the cited reports had.
unverified.cost: Autocast policy only: force fp32 for the softmax and every RMSNorm, keep fp32 accumulation in the attention reduction (PyTorch's mem-efficient SDPA backend already accumulates in fp32). Add two scalars to the existing metrics.jsonl: max |pre-softmax attention logit| and max |post-SwiGLU activation| per eval, logged per layer. Maybe 1-3% step time. No restart, no architecture change.
unverified.risk: Very low. The only real cost is throughput. The telemetry is the load-bearing half: without it there is no way to know whether the fp16 headroom is being consumed, and a dynamic loss scaler hides the problem until it does not.

unverified.name: Checkpoint EMA / WSM-style merge across the decay window
unverified.claim: Average the weights of the checkpoints spanning the decay phase instead of shipping only the last one. WSM shows a formal equivalence between LR decay and model merging (a merge can emulate cosine, linear or inverse-sqrt decay) and reports +3.5% MATH, +2.9% HumanEval, +5.5% MMLU-Pro over the WSD baseline; it identifies merge duration (the training window the merged checkpoints span) as the single most important knob, above checkpoint count or interval. The curriculum paper independently recommends EMA with alpha=0.2 over the last six checkpoints.
unverified.evidence: WSM: Decay-Free Learning Rate Schedule via Checkpoint Merging (arXiv 2507.17634). 'How Learning Rate Decay Wastes Your Best Data in Curriculum-Based LLM Pretraining' (arXiv 2511.18903), 1.5B params / 30B tokens, EMA alpha=0.2 over the last six checkpoints, +1.2% average accuracy in the mid-training setting and over 2% on MMLU/ARC-c/ARC-e/CSQA. A separate large-scale report notes offline merging gives a consistent 2-4 point gain during the stable phase but that the gap narrows once real LR decay is applied.
unverified.estimated_gain: Realistically +0.5 to +1.5% average downstream at 1.1B/100B, and a small held-out loss improvement, for zero training compute. The honest caveat is in the same sources: merging and decaying are partly redundant, so a full cosine decay to near-zero already captures much of what EMA would give. The gain is largest if the final LR is kept moderate (see the next candidate) rather than decayed to zero.
unverified.cost: Save a checkpoint every N steps through the decay phase (1.1B fp32 = ~4.4GB each; 6-8 of them is 26-35GB of disk, trivial) and average them at the end. Evaluate the merge against the final checkpoint on the held-out shard and keep whichever wins. No restart, no change to the training loop, and it can be decided after the run finishes.
unverified.risk: Almost none: it is a post-hoc operation on saved weights, so the worst case is that the merge loses to the final checkpoint and is discarded. One real gotcha: average the fp32 master weights, not the fp16 copies, and do not average optimizer state.

unverified.name: Do not decay the LR to ~0 if the best data goes last (CDMA: end LR ~1/3 of peak)
unverified.claim: A curriculum that puts the highest-quality data at the end is directly fighting the LR schedule, because that data arrives exactly when the LR is at its minimum and the model can barely move. Measured: with a constant LR, an ascending-quality curriculum substantially beats random shuffling, and the advantage shrinks monotonically as the decay gets more aggressive. Their fix (CDMA) is to set the ending LR to roughly 1/3 of peak instead of near-zero (peak 3e-3 -> end 1e-3), combined with EMA, for +1.64% average over the random-shuffle baseline and +1.2% in the mid-training setting.
unverified.evidence: 'How Learning Rate Decay Wastes Your Best Data in Curriculum-Based LLM Pretraining' (arXiv 2511.18903), 1.5B parameters, 30B tokens, benchmarks MMLU / ARC-c / ARC-e / CSQA.
unverified.estimated_gain: +1 to +1.6% average downstream at this scale, but ONLY if the decay-phase data is meaningfully better than the stable-phase data. If the last 15% is drawn from the same mixture as the first 85%, this paper's premise does not hold and the standard decay-to-0.1x is correct. It pairs with, and partly substitutes for, the EMA candidate above.
unverified.cost: One scheduler constant. Decided at the start of the decay phase, which has not begun, so there is nothing to restart. Zero compute.
unverified.risk: Moderate and worth naming: a higher terminal LR leaves the model in a noisier region, which normally costs held-out loss even when it helps benchmarks, and their measurement is at 1.5B/30B (a 20:1 ratio) versus 1.1B/100B (a 90:1, deep-overtrained ratio), where decay tends to matter more. Do not adopt this blind. The defensible version: only raise the terminal LR if the decay-phase mixture is genuinely upgraded (next candidate), and evaluate both a decayed and an EMA-merged checkpoint at the end.

unverified.name: Decay-phase mid-training anneal (Dolmino-style high-quality + instruction + math mix)
unverified.claim: Replace the last ~15% of pretraining tokens (the WSD cosine-decay leg, ~15B tokens here) with a curated mix: filtered high-quality web, instruction data, Stack-Exchange/FLAN-style QA, and a large synthetic-math component, instead of continuing the 55/23/11/8/3 pretraining mix. OLMo 2 measured average over ten benchmarks 53.0 -> 62.9 (+9.9) at 7B and 58.9 -> 68.3 (+9.4) at 13B, with GSM8K 24.1 -> 67.5 (+43.4) at 7B and 37.3 -> 75.1 at 13B, using Dolmino Mix 1124 over the final 5-10% of pretraining FLOPs. Their own ablation shows the gain is the DATA, not the decay: annealing on the unchanged pretraining mix gave only +4.4 OLMES, +2.0 MMLU and -1.5 GSM*, while adding the filtered/instruction/math data added +19.5 GSM* on the dev subset.
unverified.evidence: OLMo 2 technical report (Allen AI, Jan 2025), 7B and 13B dense models, Dolmino Mix 1124 over the final 5-10% of pretraining FLOPs with linearly decaying LR; ablation table over six candidate mixes. Same pattern independently used by MiniCPM (WSD decay stage = pretraining data + high-quality SFT data, exponential anneal over 5000 steps / 20B tokens) and by SmolLM2.
unverified.estimated_gain: Large and the highest-confidence item in this sweep. Expect the direction to hold but not the magnitude: OLMo 2's GSM8K jump comes off a 4T-token base with real latent math. For a 1.1B/100B-token model, realistic expectation is a few points of average benchmark gain and a disproportionate jump on GSM8K/MMLU-style formatted tasks, mostly because the model learns the answer format and QA register before SFT ever runs.
unverified.cost: Zero compute cost over the decay you are already going to run: it is a change to the data loader's mixture for the last ~15B tokens. Effort is the data prep: pull FineWeb-Edu's highest-quality bucket, a math set (OpenMathInstruct / NuminaMath-CoT), and a FLAN/StackExchange slice, then re-tokenize with the 49,152 BPE. One to two days of data work. No restart, no architecture change, fits Turing fp16 unchanged.
unverified.risk: Two real ones. (1) Data prep is on the critical path: the decay leg arrives at a fixed wall-clock time and if the shards are not tokenized you will either stall the run or default to the old mix. (2) Over-weighting instruction data in the decay makes the base model less of a base model and can double-count with SFT; OLMo 2 keeps it a minority of the mix, do the same. Do not put the mix change anywhere except the decay leg, or you have changed the run.

unverified.name: Weight averaging: checkpoint soup at the end of decay, and merging the post-training stages
unverified.claim: Two separate uses of the same near-free trick. (a) At the end of the decay leg, average the last N checkpoints (or N decay runs over the same mix with different data order). OLMo 2 souped three 7B annealing runs and report that across six mixes the soup equals or beats the best individual checkpoint. (b) A 1.5B/30B-token study argues aggressive LR decay actively wastes your best (last-placed) data and that a moderate final LR plus weighted averaging of final checkpoints recovers it: +1.64% average over a standard benchmark suite versus random shuffling. (c) After post-training, merging checkpoints is measurably positive: merging DPO checkpoints gave +2.8% average general performance and +2.2% safety over the base, while merging SFT checkpoints gave ~+6% general but +4.6% more harmful generations.
unverified.evidence: OLMo 2 7B (checkpoint souping across annealing runs, six mixes); arXiv 2511.18903 at 1.5B parameters / 30B tokens; multilingual merging study (arXiv 2410.10801) on SFT vs DPO checkpoint merges. Note (b) is a single small-scale paper and directly tensions with the WSD schedule already chosen.
unverified.estimated_gain: Soup of decay checkpoints: small but nearly free, on the order of a few tenths to ~1 point of average benchmark score, and it reduces run-to-run variance, which matters more than the mean when you only get one shot. Post-training merge: ~1-3 points average.
unverified.cost: Averaging state dicts of a 1.1B fp32 model is a CPU job, about 4.4 GB per checkpoint held in RAM; do it two at a time on the login node. No GPU time. Half a day of scripting. The 'N decay runs with different data order' variant costs N x the decay leg (15B tokens each) and is probably not affordable here; the cheaper version is averaging the last few checkpoints of the single decay run (EMA / LAWA-style), which costs nothing.
unverified.risk: Averaging checkpoints from a single run that are too far apart in LR space can be worse than the last checkpoint; validate on held-out loss before adopting, which you can do because it costs one eval pass. The 'don't decay all the way' recommendation is weakly supported (one paper, 1.5B/30B) and contradicts the WSD result your own 124M A/B was built on, so do NOT change the decay schedule on this evidence; take only the free averaging half.

unverified.name: Tail-EMA / Polyak weight averaging over the decay trajectory
unverified.claim: Keep a streaming EMA of the weights starting well before the end of the run and blend it into the parameters once at the final step: w_final = (1-lambda)*w + lambda*w_ema. Rationale as stated by the record author: 'under a decaying LR the late iterates orbit the local minimum rather than sit at it; the EMA averages that orbit noise away.' Modded-nanogpt optimization-track record 45 (Tail-EMA) cut the step count from 2750 to 2720 (-1.1%) at a fixed 3.28 val loss, measured over 10 non-cherry-picked seeds (mean val loss 3.278565, margin 0.00454 vs the 0.004 significance bar), with EMA_START=2000, TAU=150 steps, LAMBDA=0.6. Llama 3 averages model checkpoints produced during annealing (Polyak averaging) to make the final pretrained model. OLMo 2 averages its annealed checkpoints. LAWA-style latest-weight-averaging reaches validation targets in 15-25% fewer steps across nanoGPT-2 125M-770M and Pythia 1B-12B, with ~1% overhead.
unverified.evidence: modded-nanogpt records/track_3_optimization, record 45 (Jn2clark, 2026/06/12), 124M params, fixed-architecture fixed-data benchmark, 10 seeds; Llama 3 (8B/70B/405B); OLMo 2 (7B/13B); 'When, Where and Why to Average Weights?' (arXiv 2502.06761) and the Early-Weight-Averaging / LAWA line (arXiv 2306.03241) at 125M-12B. Note the 15-25% LAWA figure is measured under a constant or high LR, not on top of an already-decayed WSD tail, so it is an upper bound for this use.
unverified.estimated_gain: Small but essentially free and very low-variance: 0.5-2% effective, i.e. the final-loss equivalent of roughly 1-3% more tokens. Do not expect the LAWA headline number on top of a proper decay; the decay already does most of the averaging D2Z-style. The strong argument for it is the risk profile, not the size.
unverified.cost: One extra fp32 copy of the 1.1B weights (~4.4GB) held on CPU and updated every N steps with a non-blocking copy; negligible GPU memory and <1% step-time if you update every 10-20 steps. Rank 0 only. Maybe 40 lines of code. Tune tau to roughly (decay_steps / 1.2) as record 45 did, start the EMA at least 5*tau before the end.
unverified.risk: Near zero, because it is strictly optional at the end: you keep both the raw final weights and the EMA-blended weights, evaluate both on held-out loss plus the benchmark suite, and ship whichever wins. Sweep lambda in {0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0} on the held-out shard; it costs one eval pass each. The only real failure mode is starting the EMA too late (biased toward one point) or too early (dragging in high-LR weights).

unverified.name: Linear/power decay-to-zero instead of cosine-to-zero
unverified.claim: 'Straight to Zero' (Bergsma et al., Feb 2025) finds that a linear decay-to-zero (D2Z) schedule beats the common 'cosine to 10% of peak' schedule by a large margin: a 610M model at 80 tokens-per-parameter with D2Z reaches lower loss than the same model at 200 TPP with 10x decay, ~60% compute saving, and the advantage grows with TPP. The stated mechanism is that full decay to zero maximizes the effective averaging over late updates, which is the same mechanism as the EMA candidate above. Separately, 'Optimal Learning-Rate Schedules under Functional Scaling Laws' (arXiv 2602.06797) finds that once you decay to zero the exact profile barely matters: 'a broad class of profiles attains the optimal convergence rate', and that WSD is the optimal structure precisely in the hard-task regime that language modeling sits in.
unverified.evidence: arXiv 2502.15938 (111M-1.7B sweep, 610M headline, Llama2-7B at 286 TPP as a case study); arXiv 2602.06797 (theory plus supporting experiments). Both compare against cosine-to-10%, not cosine-to-zero, which is the important caveat.
unverified.estimated_gain: Essentially zero here, and that is the finding worth reporting. train/schedule.py already defaults min_lr_ratio=0.0 and neither configs/ultra.yaml nor configs/ultra_lambda.yaml overrides it, so this run already decays to true zero. The big D2Z number is a win over decaying to 10% of peak, which this run is not doing. Changing cosine-to-zero into linear-to-zero is a shape change inside the robust class 2602.06797 describes; expect <=0.5% and possibly nothing. The one thing worth doing is a cheap sanity check that min_lr_ratio really is 0 at the decay call site.
unverified.cost: One line. Or zero lines, which is the recommendation.
unverified.risk: Low either way. Flagged mainly so this does not get re-litigated later: the 60%-compute-saving headline does not apply to a run that already decays to zero, and OLMo 2 and Llama 3 both use linear-to-zero rather than cosine, so if you want to match them it is a one-line change, not a reason to do anything dramatic.

unverified.name: OLMo-2 style multi-run decay soup (anneal 3x on different data orders, average) - REJECT on cost
unverified.claim: OLMo 2 runs the annealing phase three separate times with different randomized data orders and averages the resulting models (7B: 3 x 50B tokens; 13B: 3 x 100B plus one 300B run, four checkpoints averaged). It is reported as consistently improving performance and is a genuine variance reduction, not just a regularizer.
unverified.evidence: OLMo 2 (arXiv 2501.00656), 7B and 13B. The paper states the averaging consistently improves results but the excerpt does not isolate the soup's gain from the annealing's gain, so the marginal value of the souping alone is not separately quantified in the source.
unverified.estimated_gain: Unquantified in the source and almost certainly small relative to the annealing itself, which is the part that produced the +10.6 average points.
unverified.cost: Prohibitive here. A single 15B-token decay at the measured 15-50k tokens/s is roughly 3.5-11 days on 4 cards. Three of them is an extra 1-3 weeks minimum on a shared school box with no root and a thermal power cap pending. That is the entire slack in the schedule spent on the least-quantified item on this list.
unverified.risk: The opportunity cost is the risk: those weeks are better spent on a longer stable phase or more annealing tokens. Do the single-trajectory Tail-EMA instead, which targets the same late-iterate noise for one CPU weight copy and zero extra GPU-hours. If the calendar somehow opens up, two decay runs averaged is the cheap version of this.

unverified.name: Batch-size ramp schedule - REJECT as marginal and entangled
unverified.claim: modded-nanogpt PR #163 added a batch-size schedule: same total token budget, batch size linearly ramped across three phases, giving 65 fewer steps at slightly higher per-step time (about -2 seconds on a ~2 minute run, roughly 1.7%).
unverified.evidence: modded-nanogpt PR #163 (varunneal), 124M params. The PR states the ramp was tuned to match the sliding-window size schedule and was co-optimized with the LR schedule.
unverified.estimated_gain: Roughly 1-2% at 124M under a schedule this run does not have, and probably less here. This run already uses 0.5M tokens/step, which is a sane batch for a 1.1B model at 100B tokens, so there is no obviously wrong starting point to fix.
unverified.cost: Low in code but it perturbs a job that is already running correctly, and it interacts with the LR schedule, grad accumulation, and the DDP step timing that everything else is measured against.
unverified.risk: The measured effect is entangled with the window-size schedule it was tuned alongside, so the number does not transfer cleanly. Not worth touching a healthy run for. If throughput is the goal, the flash-attention-turing swap is a 10-20% win from the same effort budget with no schedule interaction.

unverified.name: Use NorMuon (not AdamW) for SFT, or use LoRA if you use AdamW
unverified.claim: Switching optimizer families between pretraining and fine-tuning causes a measurable, SYMMETRIC degradation: "for both pretrained models, using the matched optimizer (Full-Muon for Muon-pretrained, Full-Adam for Adam-pretrained) consistently outperforms the mismatched one." The cause is the different implicit biases (Adam does steepest descent under max-norm, Muon under spectral norm), so mismatched full fine-tuning moves weights in a direction incompatible with the pretraining structure and disrupts learned knowledge. Severity scales with update strength. LoRA, by restricting the update to a low-rank subspace, substantially closes the gap in both directions across language and vision tasks.
unverified.evidence: "Can Muon Fine-tune Adam-Pretrained Models?", arXiv:2605.10468, ICML 2026 (Qu, Huang, Horvath). Figure 1 and Table 1 on NanoChat and WikiText-2, 3 seeds, plus T5-GLUE, Llama and CLIP ViT-B/32. Relative-perplexity trajectories show the mismatched optimizer ending roughly 5-10 points of relative PPL worse than matched.
unverified.estimated_gain: Directly applicable and costs nothing: MaxGPT-Ultra is pretrained with NorMuon, so SFT and the DPO policy update should stay on NorMuon (with AdamW on embeddings/1D as in pretraining) rather than defaulting to AdamW. Expect to avoid a several-percent relative degradation rather than to gain anything. Note the measurement scale is small (NanoChat), so treat the magnitude as directional.
unverified.cost: Zero. It is the optimizer you already have implemented and tuned. Lower SFT learning rate as usual (roughly 1/10 of pretraining peak).
unverified.risk: Low. The one caveat is that the paper's evidence for the Muon-pretrained direction is thinner than for the Adam-pretrained direction (the authors say resource constraints limited their Muon-pretrained experiments). Fallback if NorMuon-SFT misbehaves: AdamW + LoRA, which the paper shows is the mitigated path, not plain AdamW full fine-tuning.

unverified.name: Length-normalized DPO with an SFT-loss regularizer
unverified.claim: Two well-replicated fixes to vanilla DPO, both applicable to the planned UltraFeedback-binarized / beta=0.1 / precomputed-reference-logprobs setup. (1) Length normalization: the DPO implicit reward grows with response length, so plain DPO drifts toward unnecessarily long, lower-quality answers; normalizing the log-ratio by response length (LN-DPO) improves stability and, in length-regularized variants, gives >8% increase in length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2. (2) SFT regularization: adding the SFT negative-log-likelihood loss on the CHOSEN response as an auxiliary term (Reg-DPO / RPO-style) prevents the degradation where DPO pushes down the likelihood of both responses. Both are a few lines in the loss.
unverified.evidence: Length-normalized / length-regularized DPO: >8% LC win-rate gain on AlpacaEval 2 (RainbowPO 2410.04203 unified framework; LN-DPO analyses). Reg-DPO (2511.01450) for the SFT-loss regularizer preventing task degradation. Separate caution from a 2026 small-model study: at small scale and modest data, full-parameter SFT is the dominant lever and DPO adds only marginal gains over a strong SFT.
unverified.estimated_gain: Meaningful on chat-style win-rate evaluations, close to nil on MMLU/ARC-type benchmarks. For a 1.1B model, expect DPO's total contribution to be modest regardless; these two fixes mostly protect against DPO making things WORSE (verbosity drift, likelihood collapse) rather than adding capability.
unverified.cost: A few lines in the DPO loss function. No extra compute; the precomputed reference logprobs plan is unaffected. Both changes are free to A/B because DPO on 60k pairs at 1.1B is hours, not weeks.
unverified.risk: Low. The one thing to guard: with the SFT regularizer, tune its coefficient, since too large a weight collapses DPO back to SFT. And measure length: if mean response length rises sharply after DPO, the length fix is not working. Skepticism note: the only 2026 study I found specifically on SFT-DPO interaction in SMALL models is at GPT-2 124M on paraphrase detection and its +0.18% delta says nothing useful at 1.1B, so do not treat it as evidence either way.

unverified.name: Length-normalized DPO instead of plain DPO
unverified.claim: Both of the 2026-era small-model pipelines that report a preference-optimization comparison land on length-normalized direct alignment rather than vanilla DPO or SimPO. Tulu 3's ablation on an early SFT checkpoint with UltraFeedback (the same dataset Max plans to use): SimPO 51.8-52.9 avg, DPO 55.2, length-normalized DPO variants 53.4-57.3, against an SFT base of 55.7 -- i.e. SimPO is worse than doing nothing, plain DPO is roughly break-even, and only the length-normalized variants reliably beat the SFT checkpoint. LFM2 uses a generalized length-normalized objective (reward divided by completion length for chosen and rejected, plus a margin and an absolute-sigmoid regularizer) with beta=5.0, LR 8e-7 -> 8e-8, global batch 2048, 2 epochs on ~700k conversations.
unverified.evidence: Tulu 3 (arXiv 2411.15124) preference-algorithm ablation on UltraFeedback. LFM2 technical report (arXiv 2511.23404) for the 350M/700M/1.2B/2.6B dense family, stage 2 of a 3-stage post-training recipe, AdamW, bf16. Note LFM2's numbers are not an A/B against plain DPO; they recover standard length-normalized DPO as the omega=1, lambda=0 special case of their objective.
unverified.estimated_gain: +1 to +2 points on an instruction-following average versus plain DPO, and it removes DPO's well-documented length-inflation failure, where the model learns 'longer = preferred' and starts rambling. At 1.1B that failure mode is very visible in a chat demo.
unverified.cost: A one-line change to the DPO loss (divide each sequence's log-ratio by its token count). No extra compute. His precomputed reference logprobs are unaffected.
unverified.risk: Low. Worth pairing with the honest caveat that a separate 2026 study at 124M found DPO gives only +0.18 to +0.78 points over SFT and concluded preference optimization has 'limited marginal returns' at small scale. At 1.1B expect DPO to be a polish step, not a capability step: budget accordingly and do not let it eat the SFT budget.

unverified.name: Model merging as the last post-training step
unverified.claim: LFM2 ships a third post-training stage that is nothing but merging: train several SFT and preference-optimization candidates, then merge them in parameter space with Model Soup / Task Arithmetic / TIES / DARE / DELLA in parallel, evaluate all merges on an internal harness, and ship the best. They describe it as 'computationally inexpensive'. This is the post-training analogue of candidate 1 and it is what a 2026 small-model pipeline actually does instead of picking one checkpoint.
unverified.evidence: LFM2 technical report (arXiv 2511.23404), stage 3, applied across the 350M-2.6B dense family. They give no ablation table for the merge gain, which is the honest limitation. WSM (arXiv 2507.17634) independently reports that its merging advantage survives into post-training: +1.86% overall after SFT.
unverified.estimated_gain: Under +1 point, probably a few tenths. It is cheap enough that the right question is not whether it is worth it but whether he has time to run the extra SFT seeds.
unverified.cost: Near zero GPU. Needs 2-4 SFT/DPO variants to merge (each is cheap relative to pretraining) and an eval harness good enough to pick a winner without fooling himself. The eval harness is the real prerequisite and he needs it anyway.
unverified.risk: Low. The trap is selecting the merge on the same set he reports, which turns the +0.3 into overfitting to his own harness. Hold out a slice.

unverified.name: On-policy distillation from an open teacher after SFT
unverified.claim: Reverse-KL distillation on the student's OWN sampled trajectories is the highest-leverage 2026 post-training method at exactly the 1-2B student scale, but only under conditions Max may not meet. Measured at 1.5B-1.7B students: distilling from a same-pipeline teacher gives marginal to negligible gains, while distilling from a POST-TRAINED (RL'd) teacher recovers 80%+ of the teacher-student gap on AIME/AMC. Recommended recipe: reverse KL over student-generated trajectories, temperature 1.0, LR 1e-6, global batch 64, top-K 16 support, max response 7,168 tokens, preceded by an off-policy cold start (SFT on ~200k teacher-generated responses).
unverified.evidence: 'Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of LLMs' (arXiv 2604.13016), students R1-Distill-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B, teachers R1-Distill-7B / Qwen3-4B and RL'd variants. Nanbeige4-3B (arXiv 2512.06266) uses a related Dual-Level Preference Distillation and reports ~8% on AIME 2024/2025, ~10% on GPQA, ~30% on BFCL V4. LFM2 (arXiv 2511.23404) uses a tempered decoupled top-K=32 KD objective throughout pretraining.
unverified.estimated_gain: Potentially the largest post-training gain available, on the order of 5-10 points on reasoning benchmarks. But the paper's own success conditions are strict: student and teacher need compatible reasoning patterns (~70%+ initial overlap), and teacher reward quality degrades past ~7k-token trajectories.
unverified.cost: Needs a teacher running inference alongside the student on Turing fp16 24GB cards, which is the binding constraint. A 4B teacher in fp16 is ~8GB of weights plus KV cache, feasible on a spare Titan but it competes with whatever else is on the shared box. Plus generating ~200k cold-start responses.
unverified.risk: Flag this one to Max explicitly rather than just recommending it. The whole premise of the project is a from-scratch model; a distilled model's reasoning ability is largely borrowed from Qwen or DeepSeek, and that is a different claim to make in a capstone writeup than 'I trained this'. It is defensible if stated (frontier labs all do it), but it should be a deliberate choice, not a quiet one. Technically the risk is entropy collapse if the prompt set is too close to the teacher's post-training distribution; the paper says to mix in out-of-distribution prompts.

unverified.name: Replace UltraChat 200k + OASST with SmolTalk2-SFT (no-think subset) or TuluTalk
unverified.claim: UltraChat+OASST is a 2023-2024 mixture and is now a strict subset of what the open mixes contain. In the only controlled side-by-side at your scale (same base, same hyperparameters, 14 benchmarks, lm-eval-harness), SmolLM2-1.7B base scored 31.13 overall, Tulu-3-SFT-Mix 35.16, SmolTalk 35.49, Orca-AgentInstruct 32.42. The curated recombination TuluTalk matches or beats both sources with 14% fewer samples than Tulu and 23% fewer than SmolTalk. SmolTalk2 (the SmolLM3 mixture, Sep 2025) is the current version: 3.38M SFT rows split into a 1.5M 'think' half and a 1.9M 'no-think' half (reasoning traces stripped), decontaminated against the eval benchmarks.
unverified.evidence: 'Fixing It in Post' (NeurIPS 2025 D&B, arXiv 2506.06522), Table 1, Llama-3.1-8B and SmolLM2-1.7B, 12 Open-LLM-Leaderboard v1/v2 tasks + HumanEval/HumanEval+. SmolTalk2 dataset card (HuggingFaceTB), used for SmolLM3-3B.
unverified.estimated_gain: About +4 average points over an untuned base at 1.7B, and roughly +0.3 to +1 point over Tulu-3-SFT-Mix. Versus UltraChat+OASST specifically the delta is larger but was not measured head-to-head in this study. Take the no-think half only: a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens cannot produce useful long chain-of-thought, and training it to emit reasoning traces will cost you quality, not buy it.
unverified.cost: Free data. The real cost is tokens: 1.9M no-think conversations is far more than you want for 1.1B. Subsample to ~200-400k conversations (SmolLM2 used ~1M at 1.7B; scale down). Two epochs at seq 2048, packed, on 4 Titan RTX is roughly a day. Requires re-tokenizing with your 49,152 byte-level BPE and emitting ChatML with assistant-only loss, which you already planned.
unverified.risk: Low. Watch two things: (1) the mixes contain long-context and tool-calling subsets that are wasted on a 2048-context non-agentic model, drop them; (2) decontamination was done against THEIR eval set, so re-run n-gram decontamination against whatever you evaluate on. Expect code benchmarks to stay near zero regardless: SmolLM2-1.7B after SFT scored HumanEval pass@1 = 1.83 on both Tulu and SmolTalk. Do not read that as a data problem.

unverified.name: Use UltraMix-190k (or Tulu-3 preference mix) instead of raw UltraFeedback-binarized for DPO
unverified.claim: The head-to-head at ~1B scale is the most directly applicable measurement in this whole sweep. OLMo-2-1B-SFT, fixed hyperparameters, length-normalized DPO, 14 benchmarks, overall average: SFT baseline 33.29, HelpSteer 34.99, Code-Preference-Pairs 35.30, UltraFeedback 35.68, ORPO-mix 36.56, TuluDPO 37.63, UltraMix-190k 38.74. Per-benchmark at 1B, SFT -> UltraMix-190k: IFEval 53.49 -> 67.13 (+13.6), GSM8K 37.15 -> 52.36 (+15.2), HumanEval 19.88 -> 31.51, MMLU 40.62 -> 42.17. SmolLM2-1.7B-SFT shows the same ordering with smaller deltas (34.04 -> 36.57), and notably HelpSteer (33.66) and Code-Preference-Pairs (32.63) both made it WORSE than no DPO at all.
unverified.evidence: 'When Data is the Algorithm: A Systematic Study and Curation of Preference Optimization Datasets' (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2511.10985), 8 models from 1B to 8B including OLMo-2-1B-SFT and SmolLM-2-1.7B-SFT, 5 source preference datasets plus 3 curated mixtures, lm-eval-harness, length-normalized DPO throughout. UltraMix is 190k pairs, 30% smaller than TuluDPO's 270k.
unverified.estimated_gain: This is the single largest measured post-training lever at your scale. Expect the ordering to transfer even if the absolute numbers do not (OLMo-2-1B saw ~4T pretraining tokens against your 100B). Realistic: +2 to +5 points average, with the bulk of it on IFEval, i.e. the model actually following the instruction, which is the thing a demo GUI shows.
unverified.cost: Free data, 190k pairs. DPO at 1.1B with a frozen reference: you already plan precomputed reference logprobs, so peak memory is one policy (fp32 master + fp16 compute, ~13-18 GB with optimizer state) and no reference model resident. Fits on a 24 GB Titan. One epoch, ~a few hours on 4 cards. Effort: a day, mostly re-tokenization.
unverified.risk: Two. (1) Precompute reference logprobs in fp32 and store them fp32: DPO's loss is a difference of log-prob differences and computing it under fp16 autocast with a beta of 0.1 will eat the signal in rounding noise. This is a genuine Turing-specific trap. (2) Do not chase the code subset: Code-Preference-Pairs actively hurt both small models. (3) UltraMix curation used Magpie annotations from a 70B judge, so you are consuming their labels, not reproducing them, which is fine and free.

unverified.name: Length-normalized DPO, and skip the SimPO/ORPO/KTO/IPO zoo entirely
unverified.claim: Use Tulu 3's length-normalized DPO loss (open-instruct dpo_loss_type=norm) and stop there. Tulu 3 reports LN-DPO overall 47.3 vs vanilla DPO 46.2 vs SFT baseline 42.6, with the gain concentrated in math and code, and found it beat PPO, DPO and SimPO in their ablations. The 2026 controlled study is blunter: across 51 post-training algorithms and a 20-variant DPO taxonomy, evaluated with 5 seeds and 100 runs at 1.5B plus runs at 0.5B and 7B, 'none of 20 DPO variants significantly outperform vanilla DPO after Bonferroni correction', and the variance decomposition is model scale ~50pp >> training paradigm ~10pp >> online vs offline ~9pp >> loss function ~1pp.
unverified.evidence: Tulu 3 (arXiv 2411.15124, Allen AI, 8B/70B) for the LN-DPO numbers; 'Do Post-Training Algorithms Actually Differ? A Controlled Study' (arXiv 2603.19335) for the null result, at 0.5B / 1.5B / 7B on GSM8K, MATH and general-domain evals. That study also finds the ranking inverts with scale (SGRPO best at 1.5B with 58.0 GSM8K, SimPO worst-to-best by 7B at 85.8), which is itself a reason not to trust a SimPO headline number measured at 8B.
unverified.estimated_gain: Roughly +1 point average over vanilla DPO, and roughly zero for every alternative acronym. The value here is negative-space: it saves you two weeks of implementing and tuning SimPO/ORPO/KTO for an effect smaller than your eval noise floor.
unverified.cost: One line. Length normalization is dividing the per-sequence logprob sum by token count in the existing DPO loss. Zero extra memory, zero extra compute.
unverified.risk: Near zero. The one caveat worth stating: the widely-quoted 'SimPO beats DPO by 6.4 on AlpacaEval 2 and 7.5 on Arena-Hard' number is from the SimPO paper's own 8B/Gemma setting on LLM-judged win-rate benchmarks, which are exactly the benchmarks a 1.1B model cannot be measured on reliably. Do not port it.

unverified.name: Build extra preference pairs by delta learning: two locally-runnable open models of different sizes
unverified.claim: You do not need a reward model or an API to make preference data. Generate the chosen response with a mid-size open instruct model and the rejected response with a clearly smaller one on your own SFT prompts; the quality GAP is the training signal, and it works even when both generators are weaker than the model being tuned. Measured: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on UltraFeedback-Weak (all responses from models below its own Arena Elo) went MMLU 62.9 -> 64.0 and AlpacaEval2 18.7 -> 22.4 under DPO, while SFT on the very same chosen responses went DOWN to 61.8 / 12.3. At 8B, pairing Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct greedy outputs (chosen) against Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (rejected) matched Tulu 3's full GPT-4o-distilled recipe across an 11-benchmark suite. The GSM8K illustration: chosen-generator 75.7%, rejected-generator 44.4%, student 76.0% -> 81.5% after DPO, while SFT on the chosen data gave 70.3%.
unverified.evidence: 'The Delta Learning Hypothesis' (COLM 2025, arXiv 2507.06187), UW/AI2/CMU. Independently, this is how the SmolTalk2 preference set was actually built for SmolLM3: chosen from Qwen3-32B, rejected from Qwen3-0.6B, 447k pairs.
unverified.estimated_gain: Comparable to a strong curated preference set, at zero data cost and with prompts you control (so the pairs are on your distribution rather than Tulu's). Best used as a supplement to UltraMix, not a replacement. Expect a couple of average points, concentrated in instruction following.
unverified.cost: Generation only, and it is offline. vLLM supports sm_75 (Titan RTX is explicitly in the supported list) and AWQ int4 is the practical format there, so a Qwen3-4B or 8B chosen-generator and a 0.6B rejected-generator both fit comfortably on one 24 GB card. Budget one card-day for ~100k pairs at 2048 tokens. Do it on spare cards while pretraining continues, or between the pretraining and SFT stages. Effort: two days.
unverified.risk: Moderate and worth naming. (1) The generators' tokenizers are irrelevant here (you are consuming text, not logits), so unlike distillation this does NOT collide with your custom 49,152 BPE. (2) The delta must be real: pairing two models that are close in ability gives you noise. Use at least a 4-5x parameter gap and verify the gap on a held-out set of your prompts before generating at scale. (3) The paper's condition is that the chosen response is 'not significantly worse than the base model', which for a 1.1B student is a very low bar, so this is if anything easier at your scale than at theirs.

unverified.name: Do NOT run GRPO/RLVR on math or code for this model
unverified.claim: RLVR sharpens the base model's existing distribution, it does not extend it. Measured with pass@k: RLVR models beat their base at k=1 but the BASE wins at large k, and the reasoning boundary narrows as RLVR training proceeds; every path the RL model finds was already in the base model's sample space. The small-scale RLVR successes are real but start from bases that are not yours: Qwen2.5-0.5B went 33.13% -> 63.73% on GSM8K under GRPO with process rewards (53.75% with outcome-only rewards), but Qwen2.5-0.5B was pretrained on ~18T heavily math-filtered tokens and already scored 33% zero-shot. Your 1.1B/100B-token model will not have that latent competence to elicit. For calibration, SmolLM2-1.7B after a full high-quality SFT scored HumanEval pass@1 = 1.83.
unverified.evidence: 'Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?' (ICML 2025 + NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2504.13837), across model families, RL algorithms, and math/code/visual benchmarks. Reward-granularity study: arXiv 2607.02869, Qwen2.5-0.5B, GSM8K, VERL+vLLM, 1x A100 80GB, 5 epochs / 580 steps. 'Fixing It in Post' for the 1.7B HumanEval figure.
unverified.estimated_gain: Near zero on quality for this model, and negative on schedule. Also note the process-reward variant that produced the good 0.5B number needs a step-level verifier or PRM, which is a second model you would have to obtain, run and trust.
unverified.cost: What it would cost if you did it anyway: GRPO needs fast rollouts co-resident with training. On 4-8 Turing cards with no FlashAttention-2 you would be splitting the cards between a vLLM server and the trainer, roughly halving throughput, for one to two weeks of implementation. That is the entire budget you would otherwise spend on SFT + DPO + evaluation.
unverified.risk: The tempting version is doing it 'just for the answer format'. If format is what you want, a few thousand GSM8K chain-of-thought examples in the SFT mix buys the same formatting for a day of work and no RL infrastructure. Revisit RLVR only if a future run has a base that already scores meaningfully above zero on GSM8K before any RL.

unverified.name: SFT mechanics: block-diagonal packing masks, plus a small non-zero prompt-loss weight
unverified.claim: Two cheap knobs on the SFT step you are already going to run. (1) If you pack multiple conversations into a 2048-token sequence, tokens from one conversation attend to tokens of another unless you supply a block-diagonal attention mask; separator tokens do not fix this. Threshold Filtering Packing (which combines masked packing with related-sample grouping) measured up to +7% on GSM8K and +4% on HumanEval over naive packing. (2) Assistant-only loss (prompt loss weight 0) is the right default for long completions, but a small non-zero PLW of 0.01-0.5 measurably beats PLW=0 on short-completion data for multiple-choice and short-generation benchmarks, with a statistically significant negative quadratic relationship between PLW and score.
unverified.evidence: 'Efficient Sequence Packing without Cross-contamination' (arXiv 2107.02027) for the mechanism and the finding that separator tokens do not mitigate it; Threshold Filtering Packing (arXiv 2408.09327, NAACL 2025) for the GSM8K/HumanEval deltas; 'Instruction Fine-Tuning: Does Prompt Loss Matter?' (EMNLP 2024, arXiv 2401.13586) for the PLW result.
unverified.estimated_gain: Packing masks: this is a correctness fix, not an optimization. If you pack without masking you are silently training on cross-document attention and the loss looks fine. Call it a few points on generation benchmarks. PLW: a fraction of a point, only worth touching if your SFT mix is short-completion heavy.
unverified.cost: Packing masks on Turing: you have no FlashAttention-2 and therefore no varlen cu_seqlens path, so build the block-diagonal mask yourself and pass it to torch SDPA's memory-efficient backend. At seq 2048 a per-sequence bool mask is 4 MB, trivial. Half a day. The simpler alternative is not to pack at all and pad instead, which costs throughput but is unambiguously correct. PLW is a scalar in the loss.
unverified.risk: Low. Verify the mask actually applies: set PLW and mask, then confirm that a token in conversation B has exactly zero attention weight on conversation A for a single batch. This is the class of bug that passes every test because nothing asserts its absence.

unverified.name: Replay 5-20% pretraining data during SFT
unverified.claim: Mixing generic pretraining data into the SFT batches does not merely limit forgetting, it improves target-domain performance. Measured target-data efficiency gains of up to 1.87x for fine-tuning and 2.06x for mid-training in a controlled setting (150M-parameter models, 4M target tokens inside 4B total tokens), carrying to 8B models on real tasks: +4.5% on agentic web navigation and +2% on Basque QA. The paper's own qualifier is the one that matters for you: 'replay helps more when there is less target data present in pre-training'.
unverified.evidence: 'Replaying pre-training data improves fine-tuning' (arXiv 2603.04964), controlled 150M study plus 8B application results.
unverified.estimated_gain: Small to moderate, and unusually well-matched to your situation: a 1.1B model with only 100B tokens of pretraining is exactly the regime where SFT on 200-400k conversations can visibly damage the base distribution. Expect it to show up as the model retaining knowledge benchmarks (MMLU, ARC) through SFT rather than as a headline chat gain.
unverified.cost: Effectively free. The tokenized FineWeb-Edu shards are already on disk and already in your loader's format; this is a mixture ratio in the SFT data loader. An hour of work. No memory or throughput cost.
unverified.risk: Low. Replay tokens dilute the SFT signal, so if you hold total SFT tokens fixed you are trading instruction data for replay data. The paper gives no fixed ratio; start at 10% and treat it as one of the few things worth a small A/B, since an SFT run is a day, not three weeks.

unverified.name: Run SFT with NorMuon rather than switching to AdamW (optimizer-model consistency)
unverified.claim: Full fine-tuning with the SAME optimizer used in pretraining achieves a better learning-versus-forgetting tradeoff than switching optimizers or using LoRA. The mechanism claimed is that optimizers regularize activations differently and therefore shape the loss landscape around the pretrained checkpoint; fine-tuning with a mismatched optimizer fights that geometry. Since your pretraining uses NorMuon for 2D parameters and AdamW for embeddings/1D, the consistent choice is to keep exactly that split through SFT instead of doing what most SFT scripts do, which is plain AdamW everywhere.
unverified.evidence: 'Optimizer-Model Consistency: Full Finetuning with the Same Optimizer as Pretraining Forgets Less' (arXiv 2605.06654), Muon vs AdamW. Separately, NVIDIA NeMo-RL reports Muon in post-training gives minor improvements even when only applied post-training, and the largest benefit when used for both pretraining and post-training. The same paper flags a caution: Muon-trained models showed a stronger tendency toward rote memorization and did worse on some reasoning tasks.
unverified.estimated_gain: Unquantified in the abstract, so treat as low confidence on magnitude. The reason to adopt it anyway is that the cost is literally negative: you already have NorMuon implemented and tested, and using it means not writing and tuning a second optimizer path.
unverified.cost: Zero. Reuse the pretraining optimizer construction with a lower LR (SFT-scale, roughly 1e-5 to 2e-5 for the Muon-side groups, tuned on held-out loss). Memory is the same as pretraining, which you know fits in 24 GB.
unverified.risk: Low but not zero: NorMuon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization at SFT-scale learning rates is less well characterized than at pretraining LRs, and the one paper here also reports a memorization/reasoning caution for Muon-family optimizers. Keep an AdamW SFT run as the fallback and compare on held-out loss; an SFT run is cheap enough to do both.

unverified.name: Evaluation protocol: paired, seeded, error-barred; loglikelihood tasks over LLM judges
unverified.claim: At 1.1B, most of the benchmark movement you will see between two recipes is noise, and the standard practice of bolding the bigger number will mislead you. Concretely: use lm-eval-harness on loglikelihood-scored tasks (MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, TruthfulQA) where next-token probabilities eliminate sampling variance entirely; use IFEval for instruction following because it is programmatically checked rather than judged; compute question-level PAIRED differences between two models rather than comparing overall means, which is the single biggest variance reduction available; and average multiple samples per question on any generative task. Pass@1 has been measured to vary by up to 15% across 20 random seeds on small benchmarks. Avoid MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-style LLM-judge benchmarks here: scores shift with judge model, judge prompt, reference-answer setup and harness version, and a 1.1B model sits in the range where TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat scored 3.46 on MT-Bench, i.e. in the floor noise.
unverified.evidence: 'Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations' (Anthropic, arXiv 2411.00640) for the variance-reduction recipe (next-token probabilities, resampling, paired analysis, clustered standard errors). 'A Sober Look at Progress in Language Model Reasoning' (arXiv 2504.07086) for the seed-variance measurement. Benchmark suites used consistently across the 1B-scale studies cited above: Open LLM Leaderboard v1+v2 through lm-eval-harness.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only in model terms, but it is what makes every other item on this list decidable. Without paired error bars you cannot tell whether UltraMix beat UltraFeedback on YOUR model, and you will end up shipping whichever run you evaluated last.
unverified.cost: lm-eval-harness on a 1.1B fp16 model is minutes to a couple of hours per full suite on one Titan RTX. Paired analysis is a few lines of numpy over the per-question output files the harness already writes. One day to set up, then free forever.
unverified.risk: The only real risk is the opposite failure: over-evaluating and burning cards that should be training. Fix a single eval suite and a single seed policy now, before the decay leg starts, and run it at exactly three points (end of pretraining, post-SFT, post-DPO) plus a cheap held-out-loss probe continuously.

unverified.name: DPO beta 0.5 (not 0.1) and be willing to ship the SFT model
unverified.claim: DPO at ~1B is where the alignment tax actually bites, and the planned beta=0.1 is the Zephyr-7B setting, tuned at 7B. The nearest-scale published analog, SmolLM2-1.7B, ran DPO on UltraFeedback with beta=0.5, lr 1e-6, 2 epochs, and reported improvements on MT-Bench, MMLU-Pro and MATH over SFT alone. Against that: standard DPO on LLaMA-3.2-1B (HelpSteer2) reached only a 39.3% AlpacaEval win rate, and the literature reports that smaller models show a higher degradation rate from DPO training, i.e. the tax scales inversely with model size. Beta is the KL leash; a bigger beta keeps the policy nearer the SFT reference and is the direct lever on that degradation.
unverified.evidence: SmolLM2 technical report (arXiv 2502.02737), 1.7B, UltraFeedback, explicit hyperparameters; reported 1B-scale DPO degradation results (LLaMA-3.2-1B / HelpSteer2 and the grounding-degradation-by-size finding). Note the 39.3% number comes from a paper arguing for its own method, so treat it as directional evidence that 1B DPO is fragile rather than a precise constant.
unverified.estimated_gain: This prevents a regression rather than adding points. A 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens is weaker than SmolLM2-1.7B at 11T, so it sits further into the fragile regime, not less. Getting beta wrong here can cost more benchmark points than every in-flight trick above gains.
unverified.cost: Free, it is one hyperparameter. The real cost is discipline: run beta in {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, evaluate each against the SFT checkpoint on the full held-out suite (not just preference win-rate, which is exactly the metric DPO games), and keep the SFT model as a shippable fallback. Reference logprobs are already precomputed so the sweep is cheap.
unverified.risk: Low. The failure mode to watch is response-length blowup and confident nonsense, both classic DPO artifacts that a preference-based eval will not catch. Measure average response length before and after; if DPO lengthens responses substantially it is exploiting the objective.

unverified.name: Weight-space soup: average the DPO (and SFT) checkpoint back toward the base/SFT model
unverified.claim: After SFT and DPO, linearly interpolate the aligned weights back toward the SFT (or pretrained) weights and sweep the mixing coefficient: w = (1-a)*w_base + a*w_aligned. This is the standard, cheap, post-hoc mitigation for the alignment tax, and it is what Llama 3 does (souping across RM/SFT/DPO checkpoints from multiple runs). Merging is reported to give a Pareto-superior frontier on the alignment-versus-calibration trade-off, and model-soup-for-RLHF work reports it permits larger KL deviation without losing stability, improving robustness and OOD generalization. Validated on Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B and Gemma-2B across MT-Bench, Arena-Hard and UltraFeedback.
unverified.evidence: Llama 3 Herd of Models (checkpoint averaging across post-training stages); 'Navigating the Alignment-Calibration Trade-off: A Pareto-Superior Frontier via Model Merging' (arXiv 2510.17426); 'Model Soup for Better RLHF' (OpenReview). Gemma-2B is the nearest scale in that set; nothing here is measured at 1.1B specifically, which is the honest caveat.
unverified.estimated_gain: Recovers some fraction of whatever SFT and DPO cost on general benchmarks, at zero training cost. Small-to-moderate, and it is the natural partner to the beta sweep above: if DPO does regress MMLU/ARC, the soup is how you get most of it back without throwing away the chat behavior.
unverified.cost: Trivially cheap: a weighted average of two state_dicts plus one eval pass per coefficient. Sweep a in {0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 1.0}. A few GB of disk for the extra checkpoints, which you are keeping anyway. Runs on CPU.
unverified.risk: Very low, since every endpoint is retained and you pick by measurement. The only requirement is that the checkpoints be linearly connected, which holds here because SFT and DPO both start from the same pretrained initialization. Do not try to soup checkpoints from different pretraining runs.

unverified.name: SFT on SmolTalk rather than UltraChat-200k + OpenAssistant alone
unverified.claim: SmolLM2's team found existing public SFT sets underperformed at 1.7B and built SmolTalk specifically to fix it: MagPie-Ultra (1M three-turn conversations) plus task-specific sets (Smol-Constraint, Smol-Summarization, Smol-Rewrite) plus NuminaMath-CoT and MetaMathQA plus code and long-context data. They attribute their instruction-following gains to this dataset, and it is the SFT stage that feeds the DPO stage above. It is free and public on HuggingFace.
unverified.evidence: SmolLM2 technical report (arXiv 2502.02737), 1.7B decoder, the closest published analog to this project in size and in being a from-scratch open model. No independent replication at 1.1B; this is one team's dataset ablation, so weight it accordingly.
unverified.estimated_gain: Moderate on instruction-following and format adherence (IFEval / MT-Bench style), which is what a demo-able chat model is judged on, and which is precisely where a 100B-token base model is weakest. Little to no effect on raw held-out pretraining loss.
unverified.cost: A download plus a ChatML re-render. The SFT stage is already built and assistant-only loss masking already works, so this is a data swap, not new code. Keep OpenAssistant in the mix for multi-turn human-written conversations.
unverified.risk: Low technically. Two honest caveats for the writeup: MagPie-Ultra is synthetic data generated from Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct, so the resulting model's style is partly distilled rather than learned from scratch, which matters if the capstone's claim is 'from scratch'. Second, a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens will absorb the format of SmolTalk far more readily than its content; do not read format fluency as capability.

unverified.name: Gram Newton-Schulz (orthogonalize via the smaller Gram matrix, in fp16)
unverified.claim: Reformulates the Newton-Schulz iteration to operate on the square Gram matrix XX^T instead of the rectangular input. Mathematically identical output, 55% fewer FLOPs than a symmetric-GEMM implementation and 68% fewer than the standard implementation at T=5 and aspect ratio 4; 40-50% reduction in orthogonalization-step runtime on Kimi K2. Crucially for Turing: the author states it requires float16, NOT bfloat16, because fp16's extra mantissa precision within its narrower range suits matrices whose magnitudes stay near 1. Stability requires a restart after iteration 2 (to stop negative-eigenvalue amplification), safety factor 1.05 rather than 1.02 for the normalization, and implicit fp32 arithmetic instead of explicit identity-matrix adds. Validation perplexity preserved within 0.01 across Llama-430M, Qwen-600M, Gemma-1B and a 1B MoE.
unverified.evidence: Tri Dao, "Gram Newton-Schulz: A Fast, Hardware-Aware Newton-Schulz Algorithm for Muon", 2026. Measured on Llama-430M, Qwen-600M, Gemma-1B, MoE-1B and Kimi K2 (1T).
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only, quality unchanged (<=0.01 PPL). MaxGPT-Ultra's largest orthogonalized matrices are 2048x5632 (aspect 2.75) and the fused QKV/out projections, so expect roughly 40-50% off the orthogonalization step itself. On four Titan RTX cards where NS is a bigger share of step time than on H100s, plausibly 3-8% end-to-end. This is the one place on this list where fp16-only hardware is an advantage, not a handicap.
unverified.cost: A few hours to swap the NS kernel and re-verify update norms match the current implementation to ~1e-3. No extra memory (the Gram matrix is smaller than the input). Drop-in mid-run: it changes only how O_t is computed, not any optimizer state.
unverified.risk: Low but real: the fp16 normalization-order bug above lives in exactly this code path. Implement the normalize-in-fp32-then-cast order from day one. Verify by comparing ||O_t||_F and cosine similarity against the current path on a few real gradient matrices before switching.

unverified.name: 8-bit blockwise quantization of the Muon momentum buffer
unverified.claim: Blockwise 8-bit quantization of the momentum (first-moment) state for hidden-layer weight matrices, with AdamW kept at 32-bit for the 1D/embedding group. Measured 62% reduction in optimizer state footprint at 2.7B (4.27 GiB vs 11.30 GiB) with mean validation loss differing by at most 0.002 across all scales, and comparable downstream benchmarks. Quantization applies only to state stored BETWEEN iterations, so it does not require bf16 anywhere and is compatible with fp16 hardware.
unverified.evidence: "Effective Quantization of Muon Optimizer States", arXiv:2509.23106. Five GPT-2-style models: 162M, 405M, 834M, 1.4B, 2.7B. The 834M and 1.4B runs bracket MaxGPT-Ultra's 1.1B.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only, quality within 0.002 val loss (i.e. noise). The value is that 24GB Turing cards with fp32 master weights + fp32 NorMuon state for a 1.1B model are memory-tight; freeing a couple of GB per card buys a larger microbatch, which cuts the number of gradient-accumulation steps per 0.5M-token batch and directly improves the 15-50k tok/s figure. Plausibly 5-15% throughput depending on how accumulation-bound the current config is.
unverified.cost: Moderate implementation effort: blockwise quant/dequant around the momentum buffer. No root needed, pure PyTorch. Can be switched on mid-run by quantizing the existing buffer in place. Note NorMuon's second-moment state is only m(n+1), a 1/n overhead, so the win is almost entirely in the momentum matrix.
unverified.risk: Low on quality (<=0.002 across 162M-2.7B), medium on implementation. Do not combine this with the fp16 overflow audit in the same change; quantization noise in the momentum buffer looks superficially like the poisoning failure mode, and you want to be able to tell them apart.

unverified.name: Gram Newton-Schulz for NorMuon orthogonalization, and verifying NS precision on Turing
unverified.claim: Two things. (a) A correctness check that matters more than the speedup: the Newton-Schulz iteration in Muon-family optimizers is documented as stable in BFLOAT16, and the coupled-Newton alternative is documented as needing at least float32. Turing has no bf16. If the NorMuon NS iterations are currently running in fp16, they are outside the precision regime everyone else validated: fp16 has ~3 decimal digits of mantissa and a max of 65504, and NS iterates matrix products of a momentum matrix, so both overflow and spurious-negative-eigenvalue accumulation are live failure modes that would show up as slow quality drift rather than a crash. Verify the NS loop runs in fp32 on this hardware. (b) Gram Newton-Schulz reformulates the iteration on the small Gram matrix XX^T instead of the rectangular input, is mathematically identical (validation perplexity preserved within 0.01), and is 25-29% faster on dense Llama-430M / Qwen-600M shapes, up to 2x on high-aspect-ratio matrices; it wins most on MLP up/gate/down projections, which for d_model 2048 with SwiGLU 5632 is an aspect ratio of 2.75, exactly the regime it targets. It also uses fp16 deliberately with a restart after iteration 2 to suppress spurious negative eigenvalues, which is directly relevant to the no-bf16 situation.
unverified.evidence: Keller Jordan's Muon post and the Newton-Schulz literature: NS stable in bf16, coupled Newton iteration needs >= fp32. Tri Dao, 'Gram Newton-Schulz' (2026): 25-29% faster on Llama-430M/Qwen-600M, up to 2x on rectangular matrices, 40-50% orthogonalization runtime reduction at Kimi-K2 scale, ppl preserved within 0.01. NorMuon itself (2510.05491) reports 11.31% better efficiency than Muon and 21.74% than Adam at exactly 1.1B pretraining, i.e. the optimizer choice here is well-founded and only its numerics need checking.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only for the Gram reformulation: quality is provably unchanged (identical up to floating-point error). The precision CHECK, however, is a potential quality item: if NS is currently running in fp16 and silently degrading the orthogonalization, fixing it recovers whatever the 6.9% A/B win was supposed to deliver.
unverified.cost: The precision check is ten minutes: log the dtype inside the NS loop, and log max |momentum| per step to see how close fp16 is to overflow. The Gram variant is a drop-in replacement for the orthogonalization function, but the published kernels target Hopper/Blackwell; on sm_75 the benefit comes from the reduced FLOP count and symmetric-matmul structure, not from those kernels, so measure before adopting. Neither requires a restart, since the optimizer's stored state is unchanged.
unverified.risk: The check itself: none. Swapping in the Gram reformulation mid-run: low, because the update it produces is mathematically the same, but validate on a few hundred steps of held-out loss before leaving it in. Do NOT change the NS step count, epsilon, or the RMS-matching scale at the same time as the reformulation, or the two changes cannot be told apart. And since a restart is cheap right now but expensive later, this is the right week to do the precision audit.

unverified.name: Turing-specific throughput: FlashAttention-2 for sm75, fp16 DDP gradient compression, torch.compile ordering
unverified.claim: Three stacked speedups that change no math the model sees. (1) There IS a FlashAttention-2 implementation for Turing sm75 with a working BACKWARD pass: 2 kernels for dQ and dK/dV, fp16, head dims 64/96/128, causal masking, GQA and varlen all supported. Measured on T4 vs PyTorch SDPA: forward up to 2.19x non-causal / 1.95x causal, backward 1.35x / 1.51x. Head dim 128 and GQA match Max's config exactly (2048/16 heads = 128). (2) PyTorch DDP's fp16_compress_hook halves allreduce bytes for a reported 1.4-2.1x comms speedup, which matters a lot on a 10-card box with no NVLink. (3) torch.compile must wrap DDP, not the reverse, so TorchDynamo's DDPOptimizer aligns graph breaks with gradient buckets; reported +10-23% training MFU.
unverified.evidence: ssiu/flash-attention-turing (GitHub), benchmarked on T4 (same sm75 as TITAN RTX; TITAN RTX has more SMs and much more bandwidth so absolute numbers differ, the ratio should roughly hold). PyTorch DDP comm-hook docs and the PyTorch/Lightning DDP optimization guides for fp16 compression and gradient_as_bucket_view. PyTorch blog on torch.compile + distributed for the MFU range.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only, no quality change. Plausibly 1.3-1.6x end-to-end together, which on a 3-10 week run is worth 1-4 weeks. That converts directly into quality by letting him afford the longer 20% decay, more tokens, or more SFT/merge variants.
unverified.cost: Build requirements are CUDA 12.4 and torch 2.5.1 or 2.8.0. He is on torch 2.7 / cu118 with a driver 470, which is the problem: cu118 and driver 470 likely will not build or run this kernel, and he has no root to change the driver. Verify before promising anything. The DDP comm hook and the compile ordering are free and work on any version. Unsupported in that kernel: dropout, local masking, KV cache (none of which he uses in pretraining).
unverified.risk: The attention kernel swap is the one item here that can silently change numerics, so validate it: run 200 steps with and without on the same seed and data and confirm the loss curves overlap before adopting. Do NOT swap kernels mid-run without that check. fp16 gradient compression on top of fp16 autocast and loss scaling is a second place for underflow to bite; check grad norms after enabling. If the driver 470 / cu118 constraint blocks the kernel, items (2) and (3) still stand on their own and are zero-risk.

unverified.name: Fused linear cross-entropy (Liger FusedLinearCrossEntropy or Apple Cut Cross-Entropy)
unverified.claim: Never materialize the [batch x 2048 x 49152] logit tensor. CCE computes the loss and its gradient in flash memory from the single ground-truth log-probability plus an online log-sum-exp, cutting the loss's memory footprint on Gemma-2 2B from 24GB to 1MB, and the whole classifier head from 28GB to 1GB, with no reported convergence change. Liger's FusedLinearCrossEntropy is the same idea and is credited with most of its 60% memory reduction on large-vocab models; Liger reports +20% multi-GPU throughput and 4K-to-16K context scaling before OOM.
unverified.evidence: Cut Your Losses in Large-Vocabulary Language Models (arXiv 2411.09009, ICLR 2025; apple/ml-cross-entropy). Liger-Kernel README and docs (linkedin/Liger-Kernel), measured on LLaMA 3-8B, 8xA100, bf16, FSDP.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed/memory only, no quality change. Directly relevant here: the config is micro_batch 1 at 15.0GB, with mb2 measured at 19.6GB and OOMing once NorMuon's fp32 momentum (~+3GB) is added. The logit tensor at 2048x49152 in fp16 is ~200MB per sequence plus its gradient and the softmax intermediate; removing it is plausibly what buys micro_batch 2, which the project's own bench measured at 7,997 vs 7,385 tok/s (+8.3%) on one Titan. There is already a loss_chunk: 2048 setting doing a cruder version of this.
unverified.cost: One loss-function swap. Both are Triton kernels, so the real cost is verification on sm_75 + torch 2.7/cu118: Liger only claims 'the full spectrum of hardware compatibility offered by Triton' (torch>=2.1.2, triton>=2.3.0) and every published number is A100/bf16. Nothing in either kernel needs Ampere-only Triton features, but neither project tests Turing.
unverified.risk: Two real ones. (1) CCE's throughput trick skips gradient terms it deems negligible via softmax sparsity, which is an approximation; use the exact mode if the held-out loss moves at all. (2) Tied embeddings: the fused kernel must accumulate the gradient into the shared embedding weight correctly, which is exactly the case most likely to be under-tested. Validate by checking that the fused loss and gradient match the current chunked implementation to fp16 tolerance on a few real batches before adopting.

unverified.name: FlashAttention on Turing: NOT viable at head_dim 128, keep the SDPA mem-efficient backend
unverified.claim: Negative result, reported because the obvious throughput idea does not work here. FlashAttention-1 did officially list Turing (T4, RTX 2080) as supported for fp16, but with the restriction that head dim > 64 backward requires A100 or H100. This model is 2048/16 = head_dim 128, so the training backward pass is excluded. Community FA2 sm_75 forks do exist and do support backward (benchmarked at 1.2-2.4x forward over PyTorch SDPA, and they keep working at 8k/16k where standard attention OOMs), but the maintained one requires PyTorch 2.9 / CUDA 13.0 / Python 3.12.9, which cannot run on driver 470 (a CUDA 11.x driver), and its own test report lists 76 varlen failures and 2 split-KV failures.
unverified.evidence: Dao-AILab/flash-attention README ('For Turing GPUs (T4, RTX 2080), see the separate flash-attention-turing repo, which supports a core subset'); flash-attn 1.0.x release notes listing Turing support with the head-dim>64-backward restriction; KLM-corporation/flash-attention-2080ti (FA2 for sm_75, fp16 only, requires torch 2.9 / CUDA 13.0).
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only, and realistically unattainable on this box. Quoting it so it does not get re-investigated: the path to FA on Turing would be 32 heads at head_dim 64, which is a restart and would also change the GQA layout, for a speedup that PyTorch's mem-efficient SDPA backend (the cutlass kernel, which does run on sm_75 and does accumulate in fp32) already partly captures.
unverified.cost: n/a. The recommendation is to spend nothing here.
unverified.risk: The risk is in trying: building an unofficial sm_75 attention kernel against a cu118/driver-470 stack and getting a subtly wrong backward is exactly the failure that would not show up as a crash, only as a slowly worse loss curve. Not worth it mid-run.

unverified.name: Sequence-length curriculum (short-to-long) - NOT worth it here
unverified.claim: Reported as a negative so it is not revisited. Variable/short-to-long sequence curricula do deliver real throughput (shorter sequences train substantially faster; 16,384 was measured at -18.74% throughput vs 8,192) and one 1B Llama-3.1-architecture study even found pretraining at 1024 beat 2048 on average downstream metrics (48.0 vs 47.0). Continual pretraining from a short-context model is reported to save ~40% FLOPs with almost no quality loss.
unverified.evidence: Dataset Decomposition (arXiv 2405.13226, NeurIPS 2024), Bucket Pre-training (arXiv 2407.07495), and the 1B Llama3.1-architecture curriculum study reporting the 1024-vs-2048 comparison; Qwen2.5 Technical Report (arXiv 2412.15115) for the two-phase 4096-then-extend production pattern.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only, and unrealizable without a restart. The target context is 2048, so there is no long-context phase to shorten; changing the packing length mid-run would change the effective batch composition, the RoPE frequency coverage and the tokens-per-step accounting all at once, for a throughput gain that the existing micro_batch/grad_accum tuning already chases more safely.
unverified.cost: Would require rebuilding the shard packing and restarting. Not acceptable given the stated priority.
unverified.risk: Changing packed sequence length mid-run silently changes the number of documents per sequence and therefore the cross-document attention pattern the model has been learning, which is a quality change dressed up as a throughput change. Skip.

unverified.name: flash-attention-turing (real FA2 kernels on sm75) - NEW EVIDENCE, overturns 'no FlashAttention-2'
unverified.claim: The project constraints list 'no FlashAttention-2' for Turing. That is true of the official Dao-AILab repo, whose README now says: Turing users should see the separate flash-attention-turing repo. That repo (ssiu/flash-attention-turing) is a FlashAttention-2 implementation targeting Turing specifically, and it supports exactly the configuration this run needs: forward AND backward (backward split into dQ and dK/dV kernels), causal masking, GQA, variable-length sequences, and head dimensions 64 / 96 / 128 (this model is d_model 2048 / 16 heads = head_dim 128). Measured: up to 2.19x (non-causal) and 1.95x (causal) faster than PyTorch's attention on the forward pass, and 1.35x / 1.51x on the backward pass. Not supported: dropout, local mask, KV cache (none of which the pretraining loop uses).
unverified.evidence: Dao-AILab/flash-attention README (requirements section explicitly redirects Turing to the separate repo); ssiu/flash-attention-turing README (feature matrix and benchmark numbers). The current model code calls F.scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal=True (model/model.py:159), which on sm75 falls back to the mem-efficient or math backend, not a flash kernel, so the 1.5-1.95x is against the right baseline.
unverified.estimated_gain: Speed only, zero quality change: attention is exact, only the tiling and accumulation order differ. Attention is maybe 20-35% of step time at seq 2048 / d_model 2048 / 22 layers, so a 1.5-1.9x attention speedup is plausibly a 10-20% end-to-end throughput win, i.e. weeks off a 3-10 week run. It also frees activation memory (no materialized NxN matrix), which buys headroom for a larger micro-batch and therefore fewer grad-accum steps.
unverified.cost: Implementation: build a CUDA extension in the venv without root (pip install --user / venv install; needs nvcc from the cu118 toolkit, which the box has since torch 2.7 cu118 is installed). Swap the SDPA call behind a flag. Half a day including validation. Memory: strictly lower than SDPA.
unverified.risk: Medium, entirely on the engineering side, and fully testable before adoption. It is a community repo, not Dao-AILab, so before switching: (1) assert max abs/rel error of output and of dQ/dK/dV against F.scaled_dot_product_attention in fp32 on random inputs at the exact shapes used; (2) run a few hundred steps from the current checkpoint on both paths and confirm the loss curves overlap. Only swap in if both pass. The run does NOT need to restart to adopt this: it is a forward/backward kernel change, mathematically identical, so you can enable it at the next resume. Confirm fp16 support explicitly (Turing has no bf16 tensor cores, so fp16 is the only option anyway).

unverified.name: MUON+ row/column L2 normalization after orthogonalization (likely already covered by NorMuon)
unverified.claim: Inserts one normalization step after polar orthogonalization: divide each column by its Euclidean norm (X D_col^-1), each row (D_row^-1 X), or both composed. No extra optimizer state. Measured: LLaMA-60M 25.75 -> 25.25, LLaMA-130M 19.06 -> 18.65, LLaMA-350M 14.02 -> 13.41, LLaMA-1B (1.3B params, 13.1B tokens) 10.68 -> 10.31, GPT-Small 29.66 -> 27.64, GPT-Base 21.70 -> 19.98. Ablations attribute the gain to the normalization itself rather than to second-moment scaling.
unverified.evidence: MUON+, arXiv:2602.21545. GPT and LLaMA, 60M to 7B, compute-optimal budgets and up to ~200 tokens/param.
unverified.estimated_gain: Probably already obtained. NorMuon's entire mechanism is neuron-wise (i.e. row-wise) adaptive scaling applied after orthogonalization, and NorMuon's own ablation found the gain is largely attributable to the normalization step rather than to the second-moment term. MUON+ looks like the same insight arrived at independently and without second-moment state. MaxGPT-Ultra already has it in NorMuon form. I list it so the decision is recorded, not because it is a new action.
unverified.cost: n/a if already covered. Verifying takes an hour of reading the current NorMuon implementation against the MUON+ formula.
unverified.risk: The honest risk is double-counting: reading the MUON+ numbers as an ADDITIONAL 0.37 PPL available on top of NorMuon would be wrong, since MUON+ is measured against plain Muon and does not test on top of NorMuon or with Moonlight RMS-matched scaling. Do not stack the claimed gains.

unverified.name: AttnRes / Attention Residuals and Dual Attention Residuals (NEW EVIDENCE, reinforces the existing mHC rejection)
unverified.claim: Replacing the identity residual after attention with softmax attention over preceding layer outputs. The originating reports are strongly positive: Kimi's AttnRes claims consistent gains and was pretrained into Kimi Linear at 48B/3B-active on 1.4T tokens; Dual Attention Residuals reports 1B-dense validation loss 2.684 vs 2.704 (AttnRes) vs 2.716 (plain residual) on 50B FineWeb-Edu tokens, and 5.12% loss reduction at 0.5B. A controlled independent replication at the exact scale that matters here destroys it: AttnRes scores CLIMB-avg 0.4218 vs a 0.4829 baseline at 1.2B (z = -29.47, delta -0.061, 19th of 20 methods) and is still -0.067 at 3B. HyperConnections, the same family, scores z = -9.79 at 1.2B and diverges to NaN at 3B from step ~15000 with sustained grad-norm inflation.
unverified.evidence: Kimi Team, 'Attention Residuals', arXiv 2603.15031 (48B-A3B, 1.4T tokens). 'Dual Attention Residuals', arXiv 2607.18730 (0.1B-1B dense on 50B FineWeb-Edu tokens; 7B MoE on 31.46B). Against both: Tencent arXiv 2605.20798, 1.2B and 3B iso-recipe, 3-seed noise floor. The replication paper's own explanation: 'methods whose authors report benefits at much larger scale (HyperConnections at 671B MoE, AttnRes at large-MoE) do not reproduce here.'
unverified.estimated_gain: Negative. Best case at 1.1B dense it is neutral; the one controlled measurement at 1.2B says roughly -6 downstream points.
unverified.cost: Would require a full restart, plus (for DAR) -17.54% throughput and +10.7 GiB per-GPU peak memory, which does not fit 24GB Turing cards at this config.
unverified.risk: This is the strongest new evidence in the sweep and it argues for no change. It also independently confirms the existing mHC/hyper-connections rejection with a measurement rather than a judgment call, which is worth writing into TECHNIQUES.md as a rejected-alternative with a number attached.

unverified.name: Value residual and attention-output gating: calibration of the two already-adopted changes (NEW EVIDENCE, no action)
unverified.claim: Both adopted changes measure inside the noise band in the one controlled 1.2B study with a multi-seed floor. Value-Residual: CLIMB-avg 0.4846, delta +0.002, z = +0.81.
