Gated + QK-Norm: 0.4855, delta +0.003, z = +1.23. Both are below the paper's stated |z| > 2 significance line and below its R5 rule that 'any claimed gain below ~0.005 is within seed variance'. The originating papers are not wrong so much as measured differently: ResFormer reports equivalent loss with 10.4% fewer parameters and 20.3% fewer tokens at 82M-1.6B, and Qwen's Gated Attention (NeurIPS 2025 best paper) swept 30+ variants at 1.7B dense / 15B MoE on 3.5T tokens and found the per-head sigmoid post-SDPA gate consistently helps, with its clearest measured effect on attention sink and massive activations rather than on perplexity ('minimal impact on perplexity').
unverified.evidence: Tencent arXiv 2605.20798 Table 2 (1.2B, 3 seeds, sigma_base 0.00208). Zhou et al. value residual, arXiv 2410.17897 (ResFormer/SVFormer, 82M-1.6B). Qiu et al., 'Gated Attention for Large Language Models', arXiv 2505.06708, NeurIPS 2025 (1.7B dense + 15B MoE, 3.5T tokens).
unverified.estimated_gain: Realistically near zero on loss and downstream at 1.1B, not negative. The gate's defensible benefit is sink-free attention and lower activation kurtosis, which pays off at quantization time (relevant if this ever ships to the 5070 or to a browser) rather than in benchmark points.
unverified.cost: None. This is a do-nothing recommendation.
unverified.risk: Do not restart to remove them; there is no evidence of harm, the 124M A/B favored the stack, and the combined recipe (NorMuon + gate + value residual + norm scaling) was never tested as a whole by anyone else. The actionable part is expectation management for the writeup: claim the gate for sink-free/quantization-friendly attention, not for a loss win, and note that the 6.9% held-out-loss A/B result is a loss measurement in the one family where loss is least trustworthy.

unverified.name: Selective Attention (Leviathan et al., ICLR 2025)
unverified.claim: Parameter-free: subtract from the attention logits an accumulated, ReLU-rectified mask F built by cumulative-summing the logits of one existing head, so tokens can be marked as no-longer-needed by later tokens. softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d) - F)V. Zero added parameters, O(hn^2) extra work. The original paper reports ~2.3% perplexity improvement at 1.1B (d=28) on C4 with context 512, ~2.1% at 414M and ~1.6% at 98M, plus 16-47x attention-memory reduction at inference via context pruning. It is the rare method that also survives independent replication: CLIMB-avg 0.4874 at 1.2B (z = +2.15) and +0.0107 at 3B, where it ranks 4th; Selective + QK-Norm ranks 3rd at 3B (+0.0118). Per-step FLOPs were within ±0.13% of baseline in that replication.
unverified.evidence: Leviathan, Kalman & Matias, arXiv 2410.02703, ICLR 2025 (C4, sizes up to 1.1B, contexts 512/1024/2048). Independent replication at 1.2B/3B: Tencent arXiv 2605.20798 (z = +2.15, does not survive Bonferroni at m=19; p_Bonf = 0.61).
unverified.estimated_gain: Plausibly +0.5 to +1 downstream point at 1.1B on 100B tokens, and it composes with QK-Norm rather than competing with it. But it is a nominal improver that did NOT survive multiple-comparison correction, and the replication authors caution that 1.2B ordering is a weak predictor of 3B ordering (Spearman rho = -0.27 across the improver band).
unverified.cost: Very high on this hardware, which is what kills it. F is a dense n x n additive bias, so it cannot ride a fused kernel: on Turing with no FlashAttention-2 the model would materialize 2048x2048 score matrices per head per layer. The original paper also never tested it with GQA and lists multi-query/grouped-query as future work, so the interaction with 16Q/4KV is unmeasured. Plus a full restart: the pretraining run is only hours old now, but this is not free.
unverified.risk: Not worth it. The measured gain is inside the same order of magnitude as the seed noise the replication itself warns about, and the Turing kernel cost would likely cost more wall-clock than 1.1B-on-100B is worth. Worth naming in the writeup as the best-evidenced thing that the hardware ruled out, which is a stronger story than pretending it did not exist.

unverified.name: Sandwich Norm (Pre-LN + Post-LN wrapping each sublayer) and the HybridNorm trap
unverified.claim: Sandwich Norm wraps both a pre-norm and a post-norm around each sublayer. It measures at CLIMB-avg 0.4880 at 1.2B (delta +0.005, z = +2.45) and +0.0099 at 3B where it ranks 5th, and critically it trains stably at 3B. Its close cousin HybridNorm (Pre-LN attention + Post-LN FFN) looks better at 1.2B (0.4896, z = +3.19, one of only two methods to clear Bonferroni) and then diverges to NaN at 3B on all three noise-floor seeds in a narrow 2800-3500 step window, with a documented Post-LN deep-layer variance-growth signature. The separate Peri-LN line of work reports the same class of benefit from the same class of fix: linear O(L) rather than exponential variance growth, elimination of FP16 overflow from 400M to 3.2B, and up to +2.8 percentage points average across five benchmarks.
unverified.evidence: Sandwich Norm: Ding et al. 2021, replicated at 1.2B/3B in Tencent arXiv 2605.20798 Tables 2 and 3. HybridNorm: Zhuo et al. 2025, same replication, 3-seed 3B divergence. Peri-LN: arXiv 2502.02732 (400M to 3.2B, FP16 overflow eliminated, +2.8pp on five benchmarks).
unverified.estimated_gain: On the order of +0.005 CLIMB-avg (about one point of downstream average) at 1.2B, transferring to +0.010 at 3B. Real but small, and it substantially overlaps with what QK-norm plus the adopted 1/sqrt(depth) pre-norm scaling already buy.
unverified.cost: Cheap to implement (2 extra RMSNorms per sublayer, a few percent of step time) but requires a restart, which is the whole cost.
unverified.risk: Not worth a restart. The secondary finding is the one to carry forward: any future run should treat HybridNorm as disqualified (it is the textbook case of a 1.2B Bonferroni-significant result that does not survive scale-up), and should prefer Sandwich/Peri-LN placement over Post-LN-on-FFN. Since this run is fp16 on Turing, the Peri-LN FP16-overflow result is the relevant argument for a future MaxGPT, not this one.

unverified.name: LayerNorm Scaling (Curse of Depth) as a per-layer alternative to the adopted constant 1/sqrt(depth) scaling
unverified.claim: LNS scales each LayerNorm's output by 1/sqrt(l) where l is the layer index, not a constant, to stop Pre-LN's exponential variance growth with depth. Measured perplexity: LLaMA-130M 26.73→25.76, 250M 21.92→20.35, 350M 19.58→18.20, and 1B 17.02→15.71, a 7.7% perplexity reduction at the 1B scale. Hyperparameter-free, no extra parameters, negligible compute. Two caveats that matter here. First, the paper explicitly warns that 'combining LNS with Scaled Initialization diminishes the effectiveness of LNS' and recommends removing scaled init when using LNS, which directly conflicts with MaxGPT-Ultra's deep-net residual initialization plus its constant 1/sqrt(depth) pre-norm scaling. Second, the 1B result is at 8.9B training tokens, roughly 9% of this run's budget, and variance-explosion fixes systematically shrink as the token budget grows.
unverified.evidence: Sun, Song, Li, Yin, Zheng & Liu, 'The Curse of Depth in Large Language Models', arXiv 2502.05795 (NeurIPS 2025), Table 1: 130M/2.2B tokens, 250M/3.9B, 350M/6.0B, 1B/8.9B, LLaMA architecture with RMSNorm + SwiGLU, Adam, LR 5e-4 at 1B. Not in the Tencent 20-method set, so it has no independent 1-3B replication with a noise floor.
unverified.estimated_gain: Unknown at 100B tokens, and the honest read is 'less than 7.7%, possibly much less'. At 8.9B tokens a 1B model is undertrained by ~10x, which is exactly where deep-layer-underuse pathologies are most visible.
unverified.cost: A restart. Implementation itself is one line per norm.
unverified.risk: Not worth it, and the direct conflict with the already-adopted scaled init / constant depth scaling means adopting it would be a two-variable change with no A/B to justify either half. The forward-looking value is the warning: the current recipe stacks scaled init AND constant 1/sqrt(depth) pre-norm scaling, and this paper is evidence that stacking depth-scaling tricks can be subtractive rather than additive. Worth a 124M A/B before any future run, not a change to this one.

unverified.name: Softpick (rectified softmax) and ReLU-squared FFN: the two 'winners' that the hardware and the token budget cancel
unverified.claim: Softpick, softpick(z) = ReLU(softmax(z) - 1/n), is the single best-measured modification in the controlled 1.2B study: CLIMB-avg 0.4922, delta +0.009, z = +4.47, p_Bonf = 1.5e-4, and it trains stably at 3B. It reports 0% attention-sink rate at 340M and 1.8B and quantized models that beat softmax, especially at low bit widths. ReLU^2 at iso-parameter count reaches z = +2.36 at 1.2B and +0.0093 at 3B. Both are undercut for this specific run. Softpick's rank collapses from 1st at 1.2B to 6th at 3B (+0.0095, versus QK-Norm + GeGLU's +0.0169 in 1st), and its only fast implementation is a FlashAttention-2 kernel, which Turing cannot run, so on this box it is an eager n^2 attention. ReLU^2's own comparison literature reports that at 1B parameters and 100 billion training tokens the performance of SwiGLU, ReGLU and ReLU^2 'is very close', which is precisely this run's configuration.
unverified.evidence: Zuhri et al., 'Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax', arXiv 2504.20966 (340M and 1.8B; repo ships a naive implementation and an FA2 kernel modification). Replicated at 1.2B/3B in Tencent arXiv 2605.20798. ReLU^2: So et al. 2022, replicated at z = +2.36 (1.2B) / +0.0093 (3B) in the same table; GeGLU vs SwiGLU is z = +0.20, i.e. indistinguishable. The 1B/100B-token activation-convergence finding comes from the activation-function comparison literature (xIELU/DeepSeek-scaling-law study at 1.1B on 126B tokens).
unverified.estimated_gain: Softpick: perhaps +1 downstream point, but paid for with an eager-attention throughput collapse on Turing that would extend a 3-10 week run substantially. ReLU^2: roughly zero at exactly 1.1B / 100B tokens. Neither justifies a restart.
unverified.cost: Full restart for both. Softpick additionally costs the FA2 kernel path (unavailable on sm75), meaning materialized 2048x2048 attention or a hand-written Triton kernel with no root on the box to install a toolchain comfortably.
unverified.risk: Skip both. The writeup value is specific and defensible: Softpick is the best-evidenced single-token-level change published for 1-3B dense models, and the reason it is not in MaxGPT-Ultra is a Turing kernel constraint, not ignorance. That is a stronger rejected-alternative entry than the generic ones.

unverified.name: Keep tied embeddings; do not untie at 1.1B
unverified.claim: A direct check of the adopted choice, since 1.1B sits right at the crossover the literature identifies. At 1.2B, tied embeddings performed comparably to untied while using 18% fewer parameters, and untied showed higher loss and lower downstream scores when matched at 1.2B total parameters. At 400M a fully untied model reached 2.801 nats validation loss versus 2.784 tied, with the gap closing over training. The savings from tying fall below 10% somewhere in the 1-3B band, which is why Qwen3 ties at 0.6B/1.7B/4B and unties at 8B and above. A 2026 mechanistic result explains the cost: the tied matrix aligns with the output/unembedding space rather than the input embedding space, so the input side is the side that pays.
unverified.evidence: Qwen3 technical report (ties up to 4B, unties at 8B+). 'Weight Tying Biases Token Embeddings Towards the Output Space', arXiv 2603.26663. Measured 1.2B tied-vs-untied and 400M (2.784 vs 2.801 nats) comparisons from the weight-tying ablation literature.
unverified.estimated_gain: Zero, by design. This is a confirmation, not a change. With a 49,152-token vocabulary at d_model 2048 the tied matrix is ~100M parameters, about 9% of the model, which is exactly the regime where tying still pays.
unverified.cost: None.
unverified.risk: None. Included because 1.1B is the exact scale where this decision flips for larger vocabularies, and the answer for a 49k vocab is 'stay tied'. Note for the writeup: the mechanistic paper gives a real reason (input-side representation cost) rather than the usual hand-wave.

unverified.name: Do not restart for any architecture change (and new evidence on two blocks already adopted)
unverified.claim: A 2026 controlled replication of Narang et al. re-tested 20 transformer modifications at 1.2B and 3B with a three-seed noise floor (sigma_baseline = 0.00208 on a 12-task downstream average). Of the 20, only 6 nominally improved at |z|>2 and only 2 survived Bonferroni. Two modifications Max has already adopted land INSIDE the baseline noise interval at 1.2B: Gated Attention + QK-Norm at z=+1.23 (delta +0.003) and Value-Residual at z=+0.81 (delta +0.002). QK-Norm itself is real (z=+2.51, and the best performer at 3B with GeGLU). Separately, this is new and stronger evidence for the already-made mHC rejection: HyperConnections came in at z=-9.79 (delta -0.020), significantly WORSE than baseline, and diverged outright at 3B.
unverified.evidence: 'Most Transformer Modifications Still Do Not Transfer at 1-3B' (arXiv 2605.20798). Iso-recipe, iso-codebase, 1.2B models at ~23B tokens with three seeds; 13 configs re-trained at 3B (28 layers, hidden 3072) to the same ~23B-token milestone. Three of the 3B runs diverged (HybridNorm, SSMax, HyperConnections).
unverified.estimated_gain: No gain to capture. The actionable content is negative: nothing in the 2026 architecture literature clears the 1-3B noise floor by enough to justify throwing away the run. Also note the 124M A/B that chose this recipe won by 6.9% on held-out loss, which is far above this study's noise floor, and 5.21% of that is attributable to NorMuon + cautious weight decay (IMU-1's own decomposition: NorMuon -2.88%, cautious WD -0.97% further, architecture interventions only -1.64% combined at 70M). The optimizer is doing the work; the block tweaks are close to free either way.
unverified.cost: n/a.
unverified.risk: Caveats on the study: it evaluates at ~23B tokens, not 100B, and on a downstream average rather than loss; a modification that is noise at 23B can separate later. Both of Max's flagged blocks have POSITIVE sign, so there is no case for removing them either. Real risk to watch instead: the HuggingFace Smol Training Playbook reports that Muon and AdeMaMix both beat AdamW in small ablations and then proved prone to DIVERGENCE when scaled to 3B, which is why SmolLM3 shipped AdamW. Max's situation is exactly that pattern (NorMuon won at 124M, now running at 1.1B). Watch the grad-norm and loss-spike traces, and keep a rollback checkpoint cadence tight enough to recover from a divergence without losing weeks.

unverified.name: Softpick attention and Selective Attention (the only two mods that actually cleared the bar)
unverified.claim: For completeness, the two modifications that did clear the noise floor in the 1-3B replication. Softpick, a one-line change to softmax (softpick(z) = ReLU(softmax(z) - 1/n), producing exact zeros for below-uniform weights, eliminating attention sinks) scored +0.009 CLIMB-avg at 1.2B (z=+4.47, the only Bonferroni survivor that also trained stably at 3B) and +0.0095 at 3B. Selective Attention scored +2.15z at 1.2B and +0.0107 at 3B. Both change the attention computation and cannot be swapped into a live run.
unverified.evidence: arXiv 2605.20798, Table 2 (1.2B, 3 seeds, ~23B tokens) and Table 3 (3B, single seed, ~23B tokens).
unverified.estimated_gain: About +0.01 absolute on a 12-task average, i.e. roughly the same size as what free post-hoc checkpoint EMA gives. Not worth a restart.
unverified.cost: A restart: days to weeks of lost progress, and Softpick has no Turing-optimized kernel, so it would also forfeit any fused/flash attention path and cost throughput.
unverified.risk: Recommend against. The honest framing is that the best available architecture upgrade in 2026 buys about as much as one free post-hoc averaging trick that costs nothing. Note also that Softpick's original evaluation was mostly at <=340M on pretraining loss; the 1-3B replication is the first controlled downstream test.

unverified.name: Sandwich norm / attention-logit soft-capping - NOT needed, QK-norm plus the per-head gate already does it
unverified.claim: New evidence that CONFIRMS the current architecture rather than changing it, which is why it is worth stating. A controlled study that trained dozens of 7B models from scratch on 100B DCLM tokens measures the peak activation spike at 3,818 for a plain SwiGLU pre-norm baseline, and reduces it to 520 with sandwich norm, 92 with sandwich norm + QK-norm, 186 with a conditional PER-HEAD attention gate and 202 with a per-channel gate, while an unconditional gate barely helps (~1,800-1,900). Perplexity is essentially unchanged across all of them (9.8-10.1 vs 10.1 baseline). The already-adopted combination (QK-norm + per-head sigmoid output gate) is precisely the pair that suppresses the fp16-dangerous magnitudes.
unverified.evidence: 'The Spike, the Sparse and the Sink: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks' (arXiv 2603.05498, ICML 2026), Llama-style 7B from scratch, 100B DCLM tokens, C4 perplexity, plus 200B-token extensions. Corroborated by the Kaiyuan-2B fp16 report, which reaches for soft-capping and sandwich norm but explicitly says QK-normalization replaces soft-capping inside the attention layers.
unverified.estimated_gain: Zero quality gain expected from adding sandwich norm on top; the paper's own perplexity column shows these are quality-neutral interventions that trade only spike magnitude. The actionable conclusion is to NOT restart for sandwich norm or logit soft-capping, and to instead verify empirically (via the activation-max telemetry in candidate 2) that the spikes really are in the ~100-200 band rather than the ~3,800 band, which would leave ~300x fp16 headroom.
unverified.cost: Zero, because the recommendation is to change nothing architecturally. The only cost is the telemetry already proposed.
unverified.risk: The one unverified interaction: this study used a conditional per-head gate on a standard pre-norm block, not on a block that also carries a normalized value residual injecting layer-1 values into every layer. The value residual is an additional accumulation path into the residual stream and is the most plausible remaining source of activation growth in this specific model. Measure it rather than assume it.

unverified.name: Multi-token prediction (MTP) auxiliary heads - REJECT
unverified.claim: MTP (n independent output heads predicting tokens t+1..t+n) is in DeepSeek-V3, Ling-V2 and the current modded-nanogpt record, so it looks like an obvious add. The original scaling study trained 300M / 600M / 1.3B / 3B / 6.7B / 13B and states outright: 'Multi-token prediction models are worse than the baseline for small model sizes, but outperform the baseline at scale.' At 300M, 4-token MTP scored 1.0% on MBPP pass@1 versus 1.8% for the next-token baseline. Gains only appear at the top: 13B gained +4.5 points MBPP pass@1 (26.0 -> 30.5) and +1.7 HumanEval pass@1 (14.1 -> 15.8). At 7B, 4-token prediction regressed slightly on multiple-choice NLP tasks while 2-token was merely neutral.
unverified.evidence: Gloeckle et al., 'Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction' (arXiv 2404.19737), six model sizes on a common recipe. This is the best-controlled scale sweep available and 1.3B sits on the wrong side of its crossover.
unverified.estimated_gain: Negative at 1.1B. The measured crossover is somewhere between 1.3B and 3B parameters, and this model is 1.1B. Adopting it would most likely cost held-out loss, not gain it.
unverified.cost: Would require a restart (new output heads change the loss), plus n extra head matrices in memory during training. Both costs buy an expected regression.
unverified.risk: The temptation risk is real, because MTP shows up in the modded-nanogpt record list and in frontier model reports, which makes it look like consensus. It is consensus at >=3B. Do not restart for it. If inference speed via self-speculative decoding is ever wanted, an MTP head can be bolted on and trained cheaply after pretraining, which keeps the base model's quality untouched.

unverified.name: The rest of the modded-nanogpt architecture stack (value embeddings, U-net/MUDD skips, logit softcapping, sliding-window / long-short attention, bigram hash embeddings, paired-head attention) - REJECT
unverified.claim: These are the bulk of records 8-91 and they are the main reason people think a restart is worth it. Three independent lines say they do not transfer. (1) The modded-nanogpt README itself flags logit softcapping and structural impositions as 'unlikely to scale' to very large models. (2) METR's analysis of 77 records notes the scale-dependence problem directly: 'training 124M parameters likely looks very different from what matters at 100B+ scale', with scale-complementary ideas like Muon transferring and 'small-scale-only tricks likely won't'. (3) An independent reproduction that ablated ingredients one at a time concludes skip connections, the FP8 head, sliding-window masking and the cooldown schedule are 'tuned to 124M parameters at this sequence length and loss target, not generalizable recipes', while Muon, RoPE, QK-norm and ReLU-squared are the ones that travel. Crucially, the one scaling datapoint the README does offer is that scaling the 10/18/24 version to 1.5B gives GPT-2(1.5B)-level HellaSwag 2.5x more cheaply, and the 10/18/24 version is exactly Muon + RoPE + QK-norm + ReLU-squared + zero-init, i.e. the part this project already has.
unverified.evidence: modded-nanogpt README (record table and scaling note); METR, 'Evidence on AI R&D Progress from NanoGPT' (Apr 2026, 31x over 77 records, 36 contributors, with a depth/provenance breakdown showing shallow+moderate contributions drove ~21x of the 31x); Frontier Checkpoint's reproduction (per-ingredient ablations, explicitly qualitative/directional). Also relevant: the speedrun targets val loss 3.28 on roughly 5 tokens-per-parameter, while this run is ~90 TPP, so it optimizes a completely different point on the loss/compute surface.
unverified.estimated_gain: Unknown to negative at 1.1B / 100B tokens, and near-certainly not worth losing the run. The honest framing for the writeup: the speedrun's transferable core is already adopted here, and what remains is benchmark-specific.
unverified.cost: Restart. At a few hours in that is cheap in wall-clock but it resets the only irreplaceable resource in the project, which is calendar time on a shared school box.
unverified.risk: The specific trap is sliding-window / long-short attention, which looks like a pure throughput win at seq 2048 and is not: it changes what the model can attend to, it is co-tuned with the window-size warmup and YaRN in the records, and none of that is validated at 1.1B. Leave the architecture alone.

notes:
[optimizers] SEARCHED AND WORTH REJECTING (with the reason, so these are not re-researched):

- Muon^2 (arXiv:2604.09967), adaptive second-moment preconditioning BEFORE orthogonalization. Claims 40% fewer NS iterations and up to 1/4 training time, tested to 13B. Rejected: it is the same conceptual move as NorMuon (adaptivity + orthogonalization) with the order swapped, no head-to-head against NorMuon is published, and it is a restart-class change to the core update. The memory-efficient Muon^2-F variant exists but overhead numbers are not given.
- MONA (arXiv:2605.26842), Nesterov acceleration inside Muon, 1B-68B MoE up to 1T tokens. Rejected: MoE only, no exact loss deltas in the abstract, no NorMuon comparison, no overhead figures, and it is a restart-class update-rule change.
- Variance-Adaptive Muon / Muon-NSR / Muon-VS (arXiv:2601.14603). 1.33x step-to-target at Llama-1.2B, one extra variance buffer. Genuinely interesting and the right scale, but its mechanism (gradient-variance modulation) overlaps NorMuon's second-moment adaptivity, and the paper only says it is "competitive with representative adaptive Muon-family baselines" rather than beating them. Not worth a mid-run swap.
- NAMO / NAMO-D, "Adam Improves Muon" (arXiv:2602.17080). Rejected: GPT-2 only, no numbers in the abstract, no NorMuon/AdaMuon comparison. It is the same single-adaptive-stepsize idea NorMuon already implements per-neuron.
- Turbo-Muon (arXiv:2512.04632). Better NS initialization, removes one of five iterations, ~3% end-to-end. Superseded for this hardware by Gram Newton-Schulz, which gives 40-50% off the same step and explicitly prefers fp16.
- "How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need?" (arXiv:2606.00371, NVIDIA). Five CUBIC iterations match the quintic within ~1e-3 val loss (GPT-2 Small 3.2811 vs 3.2798-3.2809; Nemotron-3-Nano 1B/2B/4B within ~1e-3), 1.23-1.52x subroutine speedup. Not listed as a candidate because it is strictly dominated by Gram Newton-Schulz, AND because the paper is explicitly bfloat16-only: "No FP16 experiments are reported", and its derived lower bound l0 = 7e-3 is pinned to bf16 machine epsilon. Do not transfer its cubic5 recommendation to fp16 without re-deriving.
- SOAP / KL-SOAP (arXiv:2607.20548). New 2026 evidence at 8B dense and 3B/8B-active MoE on 1T-3T tokens, batch up to 100M tokens. It confirms SOAP keeps only "a consistent, albeit slight, edge over Muon in cross-entropy loss". That is NOT new evidence to reverse the existing SOAP rejection: a slight edge does not pay for SOAP's memory on a 24GB Turing card. The same paper's Muon hyperparameters (beta1 0.9, wd 0.1, 16 NS iterations, eps 1e-7) are at 25-100M-token batches, a regime 50-200x larger than 0.5M, so do not import beta1 0.9 from it as validation of the current setting.
- MuonClip / qk-clip (Kimi K2). Rejected as redundant: MaxGPT-Ultra already has QK-norm, which addresses the same attention-logit blowup MuonClip's qk-clip was built for.
- Hierarchical Muon (tiled NS, arXiv:2606.27216), CacheMuon (arXiv:2606.16371), DynMuon (arXiv:2605.17109), Spectral Deflation (arXiv:2609.21102), MuonQ low-bit (arXiv:2605.11396), Muown (arXiv:2605.10797), Newton-Muon (arXiv:2604.01472), AMUSE (arXiv:2605.22432), MuonAll (arXiv:2511.06086), Approximate Muon with low-rank adapters (arXiv:2608.14492). All skimmed; each is either an infra variant dominated by Gram NS, a fine-tuning-only method, or a restart-class update-rule change with no 1B-scale head-to-head against NorMuon.
- "Correction of Decoupled Weight Decay" (arXiv:2512.08217) is folded into the Muon-SW candidate rather than listed separately: it derives the same lambda ∝ eta^2 proportionality from a steady-state weight-norm argument, which corroborates arXiv:2607.23777 but adds no separate action.

CAME UP EMPTY:
- Nothing found that supersedes NorMuon at ~1B with a direct, published head-to-head win. HTMuon (+0.29 to +0.74 PPL over NorMuon) is the only paper that benchmarks against NorMuon by name, and only at 60M and 135M, not at 1B.
- No published guidance on changing the Moonlight RMS-matching constant. NorMuon and Moonlight both use 0.2 in eta_hat = 0.2*eta*sqrt(mn)/||O_t||_F; Spectral Scaling Laws explicitly provides no analysis of update-scaling constants; Practical Efficiency of Muon uses 0.2*sqrt(n). The current constant is the consensus value. Leave it.
- No paper tests a mid-run Muon-family optimizer swap or a mid-run update-rule change. Every optimizer gain in this sweep was measured on a from-scratch run. This is the single biggest gap between the literature and this project's actual constraint, and it is why I classified HTMuon as not-worth-it despite it being technically applicable without a restart.

DIRECT ANSWERS TO THE THREE SIDE QUESTIONS IN THE USER REQUEST (within my angle, optimizer/numerics only):

1. "Does the older architecture change model quality, or just speed?" Just speed, with one caveat that this sweep turned up. Turing runs the same math: fp16 matmuls with fp32 master weights and fp32 accumulate is the standard mixed-precision recipe and produces the same quality as bf16, in fact fp16 has MORE mantissa precision than bf16 (10 bits vs 7), it just has a much narrower exponent range (max 65504), which is exactly what loss scaling exists to fix. Same for the missing FlashAttention-2: FA2 is an IO-aware rewrite of the same softmax attention, not a different function. So the answer is yes, same recipe, same quality, slower. THE CAVEAT: the narrower fp16 range is not free in the Muon/Newton-Schulz code path specifically, and this is not theoretical. Two reproduced bugs (DeepSpeed #8432 and #8533) show fp16 + loss scaling + Newton-Schulz can silently zero every update or permanently NaN the momentum buffer while the run appears to continue. On bf16 hardware neither bug fires. So "same quality, just slower" is true of the architecture and false of the implementation until the fp16 path is audited. That audit is candidate #1 and is the reason I ranked it first.

2. "Was the 100B built the same as the one at home, or new random tokens? What was the split?" I cannot answer the provenance question: the data build is outside this sweep's angle and I did not inspect the repo or the Lambda box, and I will not guess. The split as stated in the task spec is 55% FineWeb-Edu-dedup, 23% Cosmopedia-v2, 11% CodeParrot code, 8% OpenWebMath, 3% Wikipedia, on 100B unique tokens. 3. "Same quality, just faster on the Titans rather than the 5070?" Faster is the part to be careful with. Four Titan RTX cards at 15-50k tok/s total is the stated figure; a single 5070 would not beat that, so the move is a real throughput win. But nothing in this sweep changes the fact that Turing costs you fp8, FlashAttention-2 and bf16, so the Titans are faster because there are four to eight of them, not because each card is faster than the 5070. Two of those (NorMuon-family updates, cautious weight decay) are already adopted here; SOAP is already rejected on memory; PowerCool is a decay-shape change covered by the D2Z candidate; RowUpdateFloor and EMA-Nesterov are single-record optimizer tweaks with no scale evidence and would require touching a running optimizer, so I did not promote them. What exists (RoPE base scaling, position interpolation, LongRoPE) is long-context-oriented and the literature specifically warns of a performance drop inside the original window after interpolation. ANSWERS TO THE THREE QUESTIONS IN THE USER REQUEST (verified against the repo, not assumed)

1. "Do the older architectures change model quality, or just the speed?" Just the speed, with one asterisk that is in your favor. Turing versus Blackwell changes which kernels and numeric formats are available, not what the model is. Same weights, same math, same recipe, same final quality; the Titans just get there at a different rate. The asterisk is fp16-versus-bf16: you are on fp16 autocast with fp32 master weights and loss scaling because Turing has no bf16 tensor cores. That is the pre-2020 industry-standard mixed-precision recipe and it was shown to match fp32 accuracy; bf16 became the default for convenience (no loss-scale tuning), not for accuracy. fp16 actually has MORE mantissa precision than bf16 (10 bits vs 7), and there is 2025 work arguing fp16 is the better choice on that basis. The only real fp16 risk is gradient overflow/underflow, which dynamic loss scaling and your existing divergence guard handle. So: same quality, and the numerics are arguably slightly better, not worse. The Titans being slower per-card is a schedule problem, not a quality problem.

2. "Was the 100B data built the same as at home, or new random tokens?" It is a NEW build, run fresh on the Lambda box (LAMBDA.md: the build runs in tmux session `data`, ~1.8M tok/s on 64 cores, ~16 hours for all 100B, resumable via data/shards/progress.json). It uses the same pipeline and the same mixture spec (data/prepare.py: PRETRAIN_MIX), and the mixed stream is seeded with seed=0 by default, so if the home build also used the default seed and the same source snapshots, the document order would be reproducible. But it is a re-stream from the HuggingFace sources, not a copy of home shards, so any drift in dataset revisions or in where the stream starts gives you different documents. It is not "new random tokens" in the sense of garbage; it is the same corpus, re-drawn. Nothing about this affects quality.

3. "What was the split again?" The brief this workflow was given says 55% FineWeb-Edu-dedup / 23% Cosmopedia-v2 / 11% code / 8% OpenWebMath / 3% Wikipedia. THAT IS NOT WHAT THE CODE SHIPS. data/prepare.py PRETRAIN_MIX is: FineWeb-Edu-dedup 0.55, Cosmopedia-v2 0.32, CodeParrot-clean 0.037, OpenWebMath 0.039, Wikipedia 0.048. No config overrides it (grepped configs/ and scripts/). So the real run has ~32% synthetic textbooks, and code and math at under 4% each rather than 11% and 8%. Two consequences worth acting on: (a) these weights are per-DOCUMENT selection probabilities, not token shares, so the realized token mix depends on mean document length per source and will differ again from the numbers above; scripts/prepare_data.py prints the realized mix at the end of the build, and data/shards/meta.json has it, so read the actual numbers off the build rather than off either list. (b) With code and math both under 4% of documents, the decay-phase annealing candidate is worth MORE, not less, than the evidence in it suggests, because it is the only remaining chance to get math and code density into this model without a restart.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE RUN: do not restart. The transferable part of the speedrun is already in the recipe. The three things worth doing are, in order: build the annealing mix before the decay starts, add Tail-EMA at readout, and validate flash-attention-turing for throughput. Everything else on this list is either already handled, a post-training decision, or a trap.
